  • NDSE2:C05 Quality, Architecture and Maintainability
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The chapter distinguishes immediate correctness from maintenance and later-change obligations. It informs regression protection that preserves expected behavior while recognizing that a passing suite is not complete quality assurance.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Show that a bounded change satisfies its new obligation without silently breaking behavior the owner expected to preserve.

When to use it

  • A maintenance change affects behavior with existing users, stored history or compatibility obligations.
  • An authorized policy delta changes some expected results while leaving other invariants intact.

When to avoid it

  • The suite simply mirrors the implementation and has no independently justified expectations.
  • Historical failures are being removed or rewritten solely to make the current candidate appear healthy.

Before you start

  • An identified baseline and a record of the current suite's results.
  • Versioned obligations and a candidate impact map that a maintainer can challenge.

How to apply it

  1. Run or inspect the baseline checks and preserve failures, skipped coverage and environment limitations.
  2. Classify expectations as unchanged invariants, revised behavior, historical behavior or uncertain requirements.
  3. Add targeted cases for the authorized delta and its boundaries while protecting expectations that should remain unchanged.
  4. Run the required regression suite on the candidate, investigating unexpected failures without assuming every failure was introduced by the patch.
  5. Present baseline and candidate outcomes with failure classifications, impact reasoning and unresolved decisions for acceptance review.

Illustrative example

A policy change lowers a limit for new requests. The regression set checks the new threshold, unchanged high-risk handling and replay of an older stored decision. One unrelated formatting test was already failing on the baseline. The maintainer records that separately and applies the project's progression policy; the agent cannot silently reformat an unrelated module simply because it encountered the failure.

What to check

  • Each changed expected result traces to an authorized delta rather than the candidate's observed output.
  • Both newly required behavior and unaffected invariants have relevant checks.
  • The report preserves pre-existing and unexplained failures, including whether they block the current decision.

Expected outputs

  • Version-scoped regression matrix and baseline comparison.
  • Candidate results, impact assessment and classified outstanding failures.

Risks and failure modes

  • A narrow impact map can omit a hidden consumer, so selected checks may need broader regression evidence.
  • Treating old behavior as inherently correct can preserve a bug as a permanent contractual expectation.

PAT:016PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Structured Drift Detection

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Detect when a retained instruction, assumption, test expectation or knowledge record no longer applies to current work. Compare explicit versions and validity scopes, assign an owner to resolve the difference, and trace affected decisions. Superseded material remains available for historical explanation while being excluded from decisions that require the current rule.

7 linked sources · 4 external sources · 3 book records. Read the associations ↓

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent a resumed task from treating yesterday's valid information as today's governing instruction.

When to use it

  • Policy, dependencies or interfaces have changed since a memory card or instruction file was written.
  • Several artifacts describe the same obligation and may have diverged in meaning or effective revision.

When to avoid it

  • The system discards old facts even when historical behavior still depends on them.
  • A simple textual mismatch is treated as sufficient authority to rewrite code or approved expectations.

Before you start

  • Records with source, revision, owner, validity scope and known renewal triggers.
  • A current authoritative reference and a way to record disputed or unknown status.

How to apply it

  1. Compare the task's current contract and environment against the applicability recorded on instructions, evidence and memory.
  2. Mark suspected drift explicitly, distinguishing superseded current guidance from historically valid observations.
  3. Trace candidate impacts through consumers, tests, decisions and handoffs; ask the responsible owner to challenge missing relationships.
  4. Refresh only the affected guidance and evidence under the authorized revision, retaining the prior record and reason for invalidation.
  5. Before resumed execution, verify that the selected context no longer presents stale or disputed material as current authority.

Illustrative example

A memory card says that new requests use an earlier approval threshold. A policy delta changes that threshold, but older stored decisions must still replay unchanged. The steward marks the card superseded for new requests, retains it for historical explanation and identifies tests needing renewal. The agent cannot solve the drift by deleting every reference to the former rule.

What to check

  • Current, historical, disputed and unknown claims are distinguishable in the retrieved context.
  • Each semantic correction has an accountable owner and an applicable revision.
  • Affected checks are renewed against the current candidate, while historical evidence remains traceable.

Expected outputs

  • Drift and invalidation register with owners and candidate impacts.
  • Refreshed context or expectations plus preserved superseded records.

Risks and failure modes

  • A dependency graph can miss a consumer and give an incomplete appearance of impact coverage.
  • Automatically selecting the newest text can privilege an unauthorized edit over an older authoritative decision.

PAT:017PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Blast Radius Containment

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Limit the consequences of an agent mistake by enforcing permitted reads, writes, external operations, resource use and duration outside the model's own requests. Design containment for the actual task and test representative denials. The result is a constrained execution profile whose residual weaknesses remain explicit, not a claim of absolute security or complete isolation.

13 linked sources · 11 external sources · 2 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (13)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

13 linked sources shown

Polimi (4)

  • W030 Workspace Topology as an Attack Vector in Agentic Coding Assistants
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Workspace topology's reported effect on injection exposure informs considering architecture alongside execution boundaries. The open-weight benchmark does not establish effective permission isolation, transfer to other agents, or comprehensive containment.

  • W053 Scanning the Harness: Configuration Exposures in AI Coding-Agent Supply Chains
    Informs practice

    Overbroad execution grants inform examining the agent harness's effective permissions rather than relying on tool names or configuration intent. The record motivates containment checks but does not demonstrate that a particular isolation mechanism is sufficient.

  • W060 Your AI, My Shell: Demystifying Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic AI Coding Editors
    Informs practice

    Unwanted command execution makes enforced operation and resource boundaries relevant independently of prompt inspection. The attack record does not prove that a particular sandbox or permission profile prevents every such effect.

  • W104 Coding with the Enemy: Can Human Developers Detect AI Agent Sabotage?
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Missed exfiltration and ineffective alerts make limiting possible external effects a concrete control to consider before relying on inspection. The simulated malicious-agent tasks do not estimate ordinary prevalence or validate a containment implementation.

Pragmatic Engineer (6)

  • P044 Real-world engineering challenges: building Cursor
    Informs practice

    The reported execution-isolation design informs treating the assistant's execution environment as a containment decision separate from its model. Details beyond the preview are unverified, so the association is not a security assurance for Cursor or a new deployment.

  • P051 Why reliability is hard at scale: learnings from infrastructure outages
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The outage comparison highlights the potential consequences of global configuration and update controls, informing where to limit the reach of a mistaken change. The retained editorial preview does not independently verify incident causes or demonstrate complete containment.

  • P067 What caused the large AWS outage?
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The DNS race and cascading shared-service dependencies identify how an apparently local change can escape its intended effect boundary. The provider's incident account informs containment questions but is not an independently reproduced failure or proof of a remedy.

  • P076 Downdetector and the real cost of no upstream dependencies
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Downdetector's continuing Cloudflare dependency despite a multi-cloud design cautions that redundant execution locations can still share a consequential failure path. The interview is a reported architectural case, not an independent resilience test.

  • P106 Reliability fail: No automated zone failover for Coinbase’s global trading service
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The zone-dependent matching-engine outage illustrates the consequences of an insufficiently bounded shared failure domain and manual recovery dependence. The disclosed architecture and public analysis are not an independent resilience test or a general failover guarantee.

  • P120 How will AI change operating systems? Part 2: Windows
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The Windows interviews' identity and isolation design informs treating the execution boundary as an operating-system responsibility rather than a model promise. The restricted preview does not verify the isolation guarantees or current availability of the described features.

    Informs practice

    The risk of invoking tools with developer privileges informs enforcing an execution boundary around possible reads, writes and external effects. The analysis does not demonstrate that a particular sandbox excludes every attack path.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep a plausible but incorrect action from reaching assets or effects that the task has no authority to change.

When to use it

  • A tool-using agent can write files, access sensitive resources or call external services.
  • Different work phases require different capabilities and should not share every possible privilege.

When to avoid it

  • A prompt is the only barrier protecting a consequential resource.
  • The proposed isolation claim is based solely on a local simulation rather than the effective deployment controls.

Before you start

  • A task-specific threat and effect map naming protected assets and accountable owners.
  • An execution layer able to enforce and revoke the selected permissions independently of generated text.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the exact targets, operations, data and duration needed for the task, including indirect effects through tools.
  2. Configure the narrowest adequate execution profile, separating read-only discovery, candidate writes and any separately authorized external action.
  3. Protect the contract, expected results and credentials from the maker's write domain.
  4. Exercise representative permitted and forbidden actions, retaining denial evidence and any enforcement gaps.
  5. Monitor actual effects and stop or revoke access when a request crosses scope, expires or exposes an unresolved boundary.

Illustrative example

An agent may inspect source files, write a candidate in a dedicated workspace and run checks against synthetic data. A request to rewrite protected expected results is denied by the execution layer, even if the agent says the change is needed to finish. The operator verifies the actual filesystem and credential controls separately from the demonstration that the broker rejects a sample request.

What to check

  • Effective permissions match the declared task profile, including inherited credentials and network access.
  • Negative tests cover meaningful forbidden reads, writes or operations and record the enforcement component.
  • Timeout, cancellation and revocation stop new effects without resetting or broadening the original authority.

Expected outputs

  • Execution profile with tested allowed and denied operations.
  • Effect and denial log with residual enforcement limitations.

Risks and failure modes

  • A permitted tool can expose a broader operation than its harmless-looking name suggests.
  • Isolation of files alone can leave shared databases, services or cost-bearing operations outside the containment boundary.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:018PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

PII and Secret Scrubbing

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Reduce unnecessary exposure of personal information and secrets before material enters an agent's context, logs, artifacts or external destination. Combine data minimization, scoped detection, controlled replacement and handling rules. Scrubbing is an imperfect transformation: a clean scan does not authorize sharing, and retained logs or re-identification clues can still cross the original data boundary.

1 linked sources · 0 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (1)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

1 linked sources shown

Earlier books (1)

  • B093 Agentic Patterns in Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates PII and Secret Scrubbing in B093 (Agentic Patterns in Practice): OCC:AGENT:18, ai-auto_eng/AI_AUTO_ENG/chapters/chapter09_patterns.tex lines 318–330. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:AGENT:18

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Give the task the least sensitive adequate input while preserving the permissions and retention rules that apply to the source data.

When to use it

  • A debugging or documentation task can use synthetic or minimized examples instead of raw production records.
  • Potentially sensitive text would otherwise be copied into prompts, diagnostics or shared artifacts.

When to avoid it

  • The destination or operation is not authorized even if selected values are removed.
  • The task requires identifying information but its access and retention conditions have not been established.

Before you start

  • A classification of the relevant data and the allowed destinations, purposes and retention periods.
  • A controlled transformation path that does not leak originals into temporary files or logs.

How to apply it

  1. Map where input may travel, including model context, tool arguments, failures, caches and exported evidence.
  2. Prefer synthetic or reduced data when it can answer the same engineering question.
  3. Apply appropriate detection and transformation rules, preserving relationships only when they are needed and permitted.
  4. Review the transformed result for missed sensitive content and for distortions that would invalidate the task's conclusions.
  5. Use the approved destination and handling process; retain or remove intermediates according to the source's actual rules.

Illustrative example

A maintainer needs an example request that reproduces a parser defect. They construct a synthetic record with the same problematic structure instead of uploading a customer log. A checker confirms that the defect still reproduces. The remaining diagnostic is reviewed for embedded credentials and retained only in the approved task record; passing the scanner does not authorize posting it to an unrelated service.

What to check

  • The minimized input still reproduces the behavior relevant to the task.
  • Checks cover the output and incidental artifacts, with known detector limitations recorded.
  • The data owner or applicable authorization permits the destination and use independently of the scrub result.

Expected outputs

  • Minimized or synthetic task input with a transformation record.
  • Handling decision and residual sensitivity or fidelity limitations.

Risks and failure modes

  • Rare values and combinations can reveal information even after obvious identifiers are removed.
  • A debugging trace or exception can reintroduce an original value after the input was successfully scrubbed.

  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:019PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Subagent Spawning and Fan-Out

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Delegate bounded, genuinely independent subtasks when their outputs can be integrated and checked within available capacity. Each subagent receives a clear target, contract revision, permissions, evidence requirements and stopping rule. Fan-out is a conditional coordination choice; the right concurrency follows dependencies and reviewer load, not a fixed or maximized worker count.

2 linked sources · 1 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (2)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

2 linked sources shown

Pragmatic Engineer (1)

  • P062 How Claude Code is built
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    The founding-engineer interviews illustrate subagents as a concrete mechanism within Claude Code's tool-using workflow. The retained preview does not establish an optimal fan-out, independence of workers or verified performance of the full implementation.

Earlier books (1)

  • B093 Agentic Patterns in Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Subagent Spawning and Fan-Out in B093 (Agentic Patterns in Practice): OCC:AGENT:19, ai-auto_eng/AI_AUTO_ENG/chapters/chapter09_patterns.tex lines 331–338. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:AGENT:19

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Use concurrency to address a real partitionable workload while preserving ownership and a coherent final result.

When to use it

  • Read-only investigations or implementation units have distinct questions and explicit integration points.
  • The coordinator can review and reconcile the expected outputs without creating a larger bottleneck.

When to avoid it

  • Several workers would need to resolve the same open policy decision.
  • The subtasks share an uncontrolled mutable target or exceed the available checking capacity.

Before you start

  • A dependency and ownership map with a named coordinator.
  • A shared authorized objective and bounded per-worker access, budget and expected output.

How to apply it

  1. Identify which work is independent and what must remain serial, including shared interfaces and authority decisions.
  2. Assign each worker a distinct deliverable, required source revision and criteria for returning evidence or escalating uncertainty.
  3. Limit concurrency according to execution and review capacity, reserving time to integrate and verify results.
  4. Track progress and reassignment explicitly; cancel or hold affected workers if the contract changes or a dependency is invalidated.
  5. Integrate the outputs against the common objective and rerun checks that cross worker boundaries before presenting the final candidate.

Illustrative example

One worker inventories a public API, another inspects its tests, and a third investigates a separate documentation gap. Their tasks are read-only and each returns source locators and uncertainties. The coordinator uses those findings to assign one implementation owner. It does not dispatch three competing edits to the same API merely because three agents are available.

What to check

  • Each active worker can name its unique target, input revision and exit condition.
  • The coordinator detects duplicate logical work and invalidates stale assignments after a relevant change.
  • The integrated result has cross-boundary evidence beyond the individual workers' completion claims.

Expected outputs

  • Assignment and dependency record with bounded worker outputs.
  • Integrated evidence and a decision on whether concurrency was worth its coordination cost.

Risks and failure modes

  • Workers can agree on an incorrect shared assumption and make that error appear corroborated.
  • Unbounded fan-out can spend budget and reviewer attention before useful intermediate findings are available.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Teams, Governance and the Engineering Organization — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:020PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

File-System as State Machine

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Represent long-running task state in explicit durable artifacts with validated transitions, controlled writes and recoverable history. The filesystem is a storage substrate, not the state machine's authority. Correct operation also requires ownership, schema validation, concurrency handling and a clear account of what was committed before interruption or restart.

7 linked sources · 3 external sources · 4 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (7)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

    Historical locators: OCC:AGENT:20

  • B107 The Ralph Loop: Persistent Progress Through Fresh Context
    Informs practice

    Persistent progress requires reconstructable state across fresh sessions. The chapter informs a file-backed state machine while warning that persistence alone does not establish convergence or authorization.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make a task's current state and legal next action reconstructable without trusting a conversational claim that a stage completed.

When to use it

  • A task must pause, resume or hand off while preserving attempts, evidence and remaining budget.
  • Several processing stages need explicit input, output and completion identities.

When to avoid it

  • Multiple writers overwrite the same status file without a concurrency or ownership protocol.
  • The mere presence of a file is interpreted as proof of approval or successful execution.

Before you start

  • A state schema with named transitions, required evidence and a responsible writer.
  • A write and recovery mechanism appropriate to the storage system and concurrency model.

How to apply it

  1. Define states such as active, waiting for evidence, held and ready for review, separating them from acceptance decisions.
  2. Associate each transition with the task, candidate revision, prior state, event identity and required supporting artifacts.
  3. Validate proposed updates and commit them through the controlled writer, retaining enough history to identify partial or repeated events.
  4. On restart, reconcile the durable state with actual artifacts and execution results; preserve spent budget rather than starting a new allowance.
  5. Reject stale, conflicting or unsupported transitions and route uncertain recovery to the designated owner.

Illustrative example

A task writes a candidate and begins a check, then the process stops before recording the result. On restart, the state reader finds no completed evidence event for that candidate. It does not mark the task ready merely because a log file exists. The controller verifies the artifacts, records the interrupted attempt and reruns the required check within the remaining budget.

What to check

  • Interrupted updates and duplicate events leave an explainable state rather than a false completion marker.
  • Only the intended writer can change protected state or authoritative records.
  • A resumed task can recover candidate identity, unresolved work, prior failures and cumulative budget.

Expected outputs

  • Versioned state and event records with artifact references.
  • Recovery procedure and explicit unsupported or disputed transitions.

Risks and failure modes

  • A compact status file can drift from the actual files unless transitions bind their identities.
  • A homemade journal can appear robust in sequential tests while failing under concurrent or interrupted writes.

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:021PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Tool Call Budget

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Cap tool use as one dimension of a bounded agent task and enforce the counter outside the model. Record consumed calls across retries, subprocesses and restarts, and check the remaining allowance before dispatch. A call limit controls activity, but calls differ in cost, duration and external effects, so it is not a complete spending or authority limit.

1 linked sources · 0 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (1)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

1 linked sources shown

Earlier books (1)

  • B093 Agentic Patterns in Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Tool Call Budget in B093 (Agentic Patterns in Practice): OCC:AGENT:21, ai-auto_eng/AI_AUTO_ENG/chapters/chapter09_patterns.tex lines 365–377. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:AGENT:21

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent unnoticed repeated tool activity and make the decision to spend another attempt explicit and inspectable.

When to use it

  • An autonomous task can repeatedly retrieve, test or invoke tools without a person deciding each step.
  • Several workers or restarts must share one cumulative task allowance.

When to avoid it

  • A call counter is being used as the only control over external writes or high-cost operations.
  • The task cannot observe tool usage reliably enough to enforce its stated cap.

Before you start

  • A controller-visible accounting rule for attempted, failed and delegated calls.
  • Separate task limits for time, cost, resource use or effects where those dimensions matter.

How to apply it

  1. Set the task's permitted call allowance and record how nested operations, retries and failures consume it.
  2. Before dispatch, check the action's authorization and reserve its budget through the execution controller.
  3. Record the call identity, purpose, outcome and actual resource information that the tool exposes.
  4. Preserve the cumulative counter across handoffs and restarts, reconciling uncertain or in-flight actions conservatively.
  5. Stop before exceeding the allowance and return the best available evidence, unresolved obligation and owner decision needed.

Illustrative example

An agent has a bounded allowance for investigating and repairing one test failure. Repeated failed retrievals still consume calls, and a delegated inspection shares the same task accounting. Before starting a long test command, the controller also checks the remaining time allowance. Reaching the call cap produces a hold with the diagnostic history; it does not permit skipping required evidence to claim completion.

What to check

  • The task cannot reset its usage by restarting, spawning a worker or renaming an attempt.
  • A rejected or failed operation follows the documented accounting rule.
  • The final record separates call count from monetary cost, duration and permitted effects.

Expected outputs

  • Persistent per-task call ledger and remaining allowance.
  • Budget-stop record with completed evidence and unresolved work.

Risks and failure modes

  • A restrictive counter can encourage oversized calls or hide many actions inside one tool invocation.
  • Counting only successful calls can reward uncontrolled retries and understate the work actually consumed.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:033 · Budget and Observability: Price the Next Attempt
  • PAT:083 · Budget-Gated Autonomy
  • PAT:084 · Escalation Protocol

Suggested companion techniques for comparison or combination; these links do not assert validated effectiveness.

PAT:022PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Trust Calibration

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Compare expressed confidence or reliance with independently assessed performance in a defined task class, then adjust how recommendations are used. Make evidence and uncertainty visible before the acceptance decision. Trust calibration is an evaluation and decision practice; a persuasive tone, a second agreeing model or a label such as high confidence does not establish calibrated correctness.

24 linked sources · 20 external sources · 4 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (24)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

24 linked sources shown

Polimi (14)

  • W002 Code with Me or for Me? How Increasing AI Automation Transforms Developer Workflows
    Cautions about practice

    Trust conclusions from twenty students cannot calibrate reliance for other developer populations. Use the study to delimit the task and population assessed, not to assign a general confidence level to agents.

  • W046 Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Higher confidence alongside less secure submissions exposes a mismatch between reliance and assessed outcome. It motivates independent outcome checks when calibrating trust; the old model and predominantly student sample limit transfer.

  • W066 Evaluating the Impact of Explainable AI on Trust in AI-Assisted Code Review
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Explanations can change perceived trust without demonstrating objectively appropriate reliance. Calibrate against independently assessed outcomes rather than explanation fluency; the small pool and proxy metrics limit the result.

  • W085 Automation Bias in Mammography: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence BI-RADS Suggestions on Reader Performance
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The clinical-imaging example challenges the assumption that expertise alone prevents misplaced reliance. It is an analogy for checking confidence against outcomes, not direct evidence about code-review performance or a tested SWE calibration intervention.

  • W087 Do as AI say: susceptibility in deployment of clinical decision-aids
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Clinical decision-aid errors illustrate a boundary to relying on professional experience as protection from misleading AI advice. Transfer to software review requires direct evidence; the record does not measure coding trust calibration.

  • W088 Trustworthiness Perceptions in Code Review: An Eye-tracking Study
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Changed gaze and subjective ratings without demonstrated accuracy changes caution against calibrating trust from presentation effects. Ten students and older tools constrain transfer, and the record does not validate outcome-based calibration.

  • W089 The Role of Domain Expertise in User Trust and the Impact of First Impressions with Intelligent Systems
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The relationship among expertise, error recognition and initial experience informs which dimensions a calibration assessment might examine. Arthropod classification is a different task, so it supplies a hypothesis to test in coding rather than a proven SWE effect.

  • W092 Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Attention changes among experienced automation users caution against assuming experience guarantees calibrated reliance. The legacy settings motivate examining independent outcomes, while transfer to coding agents still needs to be tested.

  • W093 Automating Low-Risk Code Review at Meta: RADAR, Risk Calibration, and Review Efficiency
    Informs practice

    The stated need for independent defect outcomes and monitoring informs what evidence would justify relying on a risk score. A calibrated-looking ranking alone cannot establish trustworthy selective automation.

  • W097 Programmers Are Poor and Overconfident Judges of LLM-Generated Assertions
    Cautions about practice

    The mismatch between confidence and detection of incorrect assertions makes independent outcomes necessary when assessing reliance. It does not show that reviewers' confidence alone predicts their ability to validate generated tests.

  • W105 Beyond Lexical Metrics: Sentence-Embedding Detection of Reviewer Habituation in AI Code Review
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Increasing approval rates over time cannot establish calibrated trust when defect-detection changes are unknown. Selection, learning and project dynamics remain alternative explanations, so approval trends should not replace independent outcome assessment.

  • W110 Overreliance on AI: Literature Review
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Surveyed skepticism does not necessarily predict observed reliance, so trust assessment needs behavioral outcomes as well as expressed attitudes. The noncoding literature does not establish a software-specific calibration effect.

  • W207 Putting AI on the Org Chart: Evidence on Delegation and Accountability
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    AI-employee framing and subgroup differences caution against treating an organizational label as evidence of trustworthy review. The document task and subgroup result do not establish a general code-review effect or validate calibrated reliance.

  • W213 Developer Task Delegation to LLMs and the Trust Factor: A Mixed Methods Study
    Cautions about practice

    Trust associated with delegation is not evidence that greater reliance produces better outcomes. Calibration still requires independently assessed results rather than treating self-reported confidence or delegation frequency as proof of effectiveness.

Osmani (1)

  • O056 Cognitive Surrender
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Adopting an answer without forming an independent view identifies a reliance failure that trust calibration should examine. The article's interpretation of cognition research does not establish long-term causal developer outcomes.

Pragmatic Engineer (2)

  • P042 Microsoft is dogfooding AI dev tools’ future
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Observed coding-agent failures alongside optimistic platform messaging caution against calibrating reliance from vendor demonstrations or executive claims. The situated BUILD observations and restricted preview are not a representative evaluation of agent reliability.

  • P047 Learnings from two years of using AI tools for software engineering
    Cautions about practice

    The discussion of cognitive bias in the transition to agentic assistance informs checking whether confidence and reliance follow evidence rather than convenience. The practitioner reflection is not an independently calibrated trust study.

Fowler website (3)

  • F004 In-line assistance - how can it get in the way?
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Automation bias, anchoring and reluctance to discard generated work identify ways reliance can exceed the evidence supporting a suggestion. The examples describe possible mechanisms, not measured bias frequencies or a calibrated trust model.

  • F008 How to tackle unreliability of coding assistants
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The proposed reliance decision combines feedback, ability to check an answer and consequences of error, informing how assistance should be trusted in a task. The personal heuristics and informal numbers are not calibrated reliability estimates.

  • F039 I don't like LLMs
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Fowler's separation of personal discomfort from recognized usefulness informs distinguishing reactions to conversational style from evidence-based reliance on a tool. The reflection is not a population-attitude study, error-rate estimate or recommendation to avoid LLMs altogether.

Earlier books (3)

  • B004 The Fundamental Shift
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The discussion of nondeterminism motivates calibrating reliance on generated output and keeping controls beyond code production. Its historical analogy does not establish a common reliability level for different tools.

  • B018 Antipatterns: What Not to Do
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The antipatterns describe how apparent speed and blind delegation can conceal reliability problems. They supply counterconditions for trust calibration, not estimates of their frequency or causal effect.

  • B093 Agentic Patterns in Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Trust Calibration in B093 (Agentic Patterns in Practice): OCC:AGENT:22, ai-auto_eng/AI_AUTO_ENG/chapters/chapter09_patterns.tex lines 378–385. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:AGENT:22

NDSE2 chapters (1)

  • NDSE2:C08 Code Review and Trust Calibration
    Informs practice

    Automation bias, false positives and shared blind spots make reliance a review decision rather than a reaction to fluent output. They inform trust calibration without treating reviewer agreement as independent evidence.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Help reviewers rely on useful assistance without confusing fluency, familiarity or model agreement with evidence of correctness.

When to use it

  • AI-generated findings influence whether reviewers investigate, accept or dismiss a candidate.
  • A team wants to understand when its confidence in a tool matches observed results.

When to avoid it

  • There is no independent outcome assessment against which confidence can be compared.
  • A confidence label would bypass required evidence or the responsible owner's decision.

Before you start

  • A defined unit of assessment, such as a review finding or behavior prediction.
  • Independent outcome criteria and a record of confidence or reliance before the result is known.

How to apply it

  1. Specify the claim being assessed and what would count as correct, incorrect or unresolved in the relevant setting.
  2. Record the recommendation, its evidence and uncertainty before inspecting the independent outcome, avoiding retrospective confidence labels.
  3. Evaluate the outcome using sources or checks that do not merely repeat the recommendation's assumptions.
  4. Compare confidence and actual results by meaningful task or risk group, retaining false positives, misses and unresolved cases.
  5. Adjust review routing or presentation from the observed mismatch, then reassess when the tool, task mix or evidence changes.

Illustrative example

A team records whether reviewers initially rate a model's defect claims as strong, tentative or unsupported. Maintainers then investigate the claims against the code and approved behavior. Some confident claims prove false and some tentative ones reveal real defects. The team changes how evidence is shown and tracks later decisions; it does not turn those observations into a universal accuracy rating for the model.

What to check

  • Confidence or reliance is recorded before outcomes and linked to a clearly defined claim.
  • Outcome assessment is independent enough to expose confident errors rather than rubber-stamp recommendations.
  • Reported conclusions state the task scope, unresolved cases and consequences of mistaken reliance.

Expected outputs

  • Confidence-versus-outcome record with task and evidence context.
  • Revised review guidance and a trigger for renewed assessment.

Risks and failure modes

  • Selective investigation of only confident findings can bias the apparent performance.
  • A numerical score can appear calibrated while hiding a dangerous error in a rare but consequential category.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Code Review and Trust Calibration — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:010 · Inference-Healed Code Review
  • PAT:052 · Review Gauntlet
  • PAT:075 · Convergence Review

PAT:023PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

The External Bash Loop

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Use an external shell-driven controller as one possible implementation of a bounded propose, act and observe loop. The controller maintains explicit task state, enforces permissions and budgets, and interprets typed results before another attempt. This optional companion variant describes responsibilities; it is not a production-ready Bash script or a guarantee that shell orchestration is adequate for every environment.

6 linked sources · 1 external sources · 5 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (6)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

6 linked sources shown

  • P110 What is “loop engineering?”
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The account of Ralph-style loops and scheduled harness features informs considering an external controller for repeated goal-oriented work. The discussed Osmani blog edition is the same underlying work catalogued as O012; paid details and comparative loop outcomes remain unreviewed.

Earlier books (5)

  • B056 Autonomous Loops and Behavioral Foundations

Applying that distinction to this route is an editorial reading choice; the annotation does not specify Bash or demonstrate the external-loop mechanism.

  • B088 The Ralph Loop Pattern

    The Ralph chapter repeats a task with fresh context and progress outside the model. It informs the external-loop mechanism, while a completion token or passing test remains insufficient proof of intended behavior.

  • B097 Complete Implementation Guide

    The implementation guide assembles scripts, plans, prompts and checklists for the loop. It provides operational reading for external repetition, with its production-ready label unconfirmed by execution or security audit here.

    Documents practice origin · primary reading for this source

This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:LOOP:R1

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make repetition controlled by an inspectable process instead of allowing an agent's completion text to determine whether it runs forever.

When to use it

  • A local task has simple stages whose exit conditions and artifacts can be interpreted reliably.
  • A team can evaluate whether an external controller is a sufficient and maintainable implementation route.

When to avoid it

  • The workflow needs complex concurrent recovery or external effects that the proposed controller cannot enforce safely.
  • A loop would parse free-form model text as commands or as acceptance authority.

Before you start

  • Structured task state and result statuses with persistent accounting.
  • A restricted execution environment, controlled command construction and an owner for failure recovery.

How to apply it

  1. Define the input revision, permitted operations, protected artifacts and typed exits before implementing repetition.
  2. Run one bounded attempt and collect its candidate, diagnostic, usage and outcome through a documented interface.
  3. Persist the result and remaining budget before deciding whether another attempt is eligible.
  4. Retry only for a concrete in-scope diagnostic; route ambiguity, denied authority or unsupported state to the relevant owner.
  5. Test interruption, malformed output, command failure and exhausted budget, then stop at review readiness rather than implicit acceptance.

Illustrative example

A local controller asks an agent to repair one failing example and expects a result file naming the candidate and check outcome. When the process exits without that file, the controller records an interrupted attempt and does not treat terminal text saying done as success. A later retry uses the remaining allowance and the same protected expectation; a reviewer still decides whether the candidate is acceptable.

What to check

  • Free-form output cannot become an unchecked shell command or a success transition.
  • Restarts, failed commands and malformed results preserve state and cumulative usage.
  • The controller's stop conditions can be demonstrated independently of a cooperative model response.

Expected outputs

  • Controller interface, explicit state transitions and tested failure behavior.
  • Per-attempt evidence with a final review, hold or failure status.

Risks and failure modes

  • Fragile parsing and quoting can turn ordinary model text or filenames into unintended operations.
  • A wrapper can give a false sense of control when the invoked tool retains broader permissions than the wrapper checks.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:026 · Run Until Done: Retry Against Reality
  • PAT:083 · Budget-Gated Autonomy

PAT:024PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

The Stop-Hook Loop

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Use a stop hook to inspect an agent's proposed exit and decide whether the current task has eligible next work. The hook consults durable state, evidence and remaining budget; it can allow a stop, return a bounded diagnostic or require escalation. Re-entry continues the same contract and accounting rather than granting a fresh objective or unlimited retries.

1 linked sources · 0 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (1)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

1 linked sources shown

Earlier books (1)

  • B107 The Ralph Loop: Persistent Progress Through Fresh Context
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates The Stop-Hook Loop in B107 (The Ralph Loop: Persistent Progress Through Fresh Context): OCC:LOOP:R2, NDLE/new_chapters/chapter04_ralph_loop.tex lines 545–545. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:LOOP:R2

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Avoid premature completion claims while retaining an explicit way to stop when further autonomous work is unjustified.

When to use it

  • An existing agent runtime provides a reliable exit callback and the task has machine-checkable completion prerequisites.
  • A bounded diagnostic can legitimately guide one more attempt under the same objective.

When to avoid it

  • The hook rejects every stop until the agent asserts success more convincingly.
  • A missing owner decision or permission is being treated as something another generation attempt can resolve.

Before you start

  • An understood runtime hook contract and a durable task ledger.
  • Protected expectations plus explicit retry, hold, cancellation and review-readiness outcomes.

How to apply it

  1. Define which evidence must be present for the proposed exit and which gaps require an owner rather than another attempt.
  2. At the hook, read the exact candidate state and cumulative budget instead of relying on a prose completion summary.
  3. If an in-scope diagnostic remains and budget permits, return one bounded instruction identifying the failed obligation.
  4. Preserve the same contract and oracle on re-entry, recording the hook decision and charging all work to the existing task.
  5. Allow a typed stop for exhaustion, cancellation, unclear intention or unavailable authority, retaining the unfinished obligations for handoff.

Illustrative example

An agent proposes to stop after changing a replay function. The hook finds that its required independent replay result is missing and requests that check within the remaining budget. The check reveals an unresolved policy question, so the next hook decision is a hold for the policy owner. It does not force the agent to rewrite the expected result until the exit appears green.

What to check

  • Each re-entry has a recorded diagnostic, eligibility decision and remaining allowance.
  • Cancellation and exhausted-budget exits are possible even when the task is incomplete.
  • The hook cannot modify protected expectations or convert a review-ready state into acceptance.

Expected outputs

  • Hook decision log and persistent continuation state.
  • Current candidate evidence or a clear hold with the required owner decision.

Risks and failure modes

  • Repeated automatic re-entry can conceal a loop with no new information.
  • A runtime-specific hook may miss alternate termination paths unless those paths are explicitly tested.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:025PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

The Editor-Native Manual Loop

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Use a human-guided editor session as a complete and legitimate execution route: select one scoped action, inspect its result, obtain relevant evidence and decide what happens next. The engineer controls progression while the assistant contributes drafts, explanations or diagnostics. Manual guidance is suitable when its observed overhead is lower than maintaining an additional autonomous controller.

12 linked sources · 9 external sources · 3 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (12)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

12 linked sources shown

Polimi (3)

  • W002 Code with Me or for Me? How Increasing AI Automation Transforms Developer Workflows
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The visibility constraint informs when a human-guided editor loop may be preferable to broader delegation. The record does not establish that interactive guidance is faster or that human presence guarantees trustworthy review.

  • W158 Should I Give Up Now? Investigating LLM Pitfalls in Software Engineering
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Abandonment after wrong replies, overload and context loss makes a human-guided or unassisted route a legitimate option when assistance stops helping. The chat-assistant task does not establish the limits of modern autonomous agents.

  • W213 Developer Task Delegation to LLMs and the Trust Factor: A Mixed Methods Study
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Reported choices among full delegation, partial delegation and doing work oneself inform keeping a human-guided route available. The interviews and survey describe choices, not which route is causally more effective.

Osmani (1)

  • O015 Is the IDE dead?
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The retained role of editors for targeted inspection informs choosing a human-guided session when a change needs close judgment, even if orchestration becomes asynchronous. This is a prospective control-surface argument, not a measured advantage of manual loops.

Pragmatic Engineer (2)

  • P008 IDEs with GenAI features that Software Engineers love
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The reported editor preferences can inform which human-guided tool environment to investigate for an assisted workflow. Voluntary early-adopter replies, a canonical-count discrepancy and the limited public excerpt cannot establish comparative productivity or an optimal editor choice.

  • P043 Vibe Coding as a software engineer
    Illustrates practice

    Cases where developers resume direct control illustrate a legitimate human-guided route for finishing work after agent-led exploration. The preview does not establish how often that intervention is necessary or whether it is faster.

Fowler website (3)

  • F003 In-line assistance - when is it more useful?
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The inline-assistance discussion informs when a human-guided editor loop is useful, considering familiarity, change size and the cost of checking or reworking suggestions. Experience-based guidance does not establish a universal productivity advantage.

  • F014 Guiding an LLM for Robust Java ByteBuffer Code
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    Unmesh Joshi's ByteBuffer dialogue illustrates a developer inspecting a concrete state-mutation problem and steering successive implementation choices. The improved access design does not by itself prove thread safety or performance.

  • F017 Building Custom Tooling with LLMs
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep simple or judgment-heavy changes manageable without adding coordination machinery that does not resolve a concrete uncertainty.

When to use it

  • A small change has a clear diff and a direct verification step.
  • Frequent interpretation decisions make interactive guidance useful and affordable.

When to avoid it

  • A long task loses critical state whenever the editor session closes.
  • The engineer is expected to rubber-stamp every tool action without inspecting the consequential decisions.

Before you start

  • A clear authorized objective and the existing repository permission boundaries.
  • A practical way to inspect the diff, run relevant checks and retain the final decision.

How to apply it

  1. Choose the next meaningful increment and identify what the assistant may inspect or change.
  2. Ask for a candidate or diagnostic with its assumptions visible, keeping the approved behavior separate from the proposed implementation.
  3. Inspect the changed code or artifact and run the check appropriate to its actual consequence.
  4. Use the observation to continue, revise the approach or stop for clarification; do not repeat suggestions without a new reason.
  5. Retain a short record of the final revision, evidence, unresolved issues and responsible acceptance decision.

Illustrative example

A maintainer corrects a non-authoritative help heading with assistance in the editor. They inspect the one-file diff and render the page to confirm its appearance and links. No parallel coordinator is needed. If the edit unexpectedly changes executable routing text, they pause to clarify the newly affected behavior instead of assuming the same lightweight route remains adequate.

What to check

  • The final diff stays within the agreed scope or records an authorized change to it.
  • The check answers the actual obligation, such as rendered wording or runtime behavior, rather than merely confirming that the file saved.
  • The maintainer can explain the result and what would require a stronger review route.

Expected outputs

  • Scoped candidate with proportionate verification evidence.
  • Short decision record and any trigger for reconsidering the execution route.

Risks and failure modes

  • Interactive convenience can make unrecorded assumptions difficult to recover later.
  • A confident human can still accept a plausible generated change without checking its consequential behavior.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:026PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Run Until Done: Retry Against Reality

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Retry a bounded task only when a concrete observation provides a reason to expect the next attempt to address an identified failure. Preserve the authorized objective and protected expectations, record the attempted remedy and recheck the candidate. Done means reaching the appropriate reviewed state or a named stop, not an assumption that enough retries must eventually converge.

8 linked sources · 7 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (8)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

8 linked sources shown

  • W042 Security Degradation in Iterative AI Code Generation: A Systematic Analysis of the Paradox
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Accumulating vulnerabilities during improvement iterations directly cautions against equating repeated generation with convergence to an acceptable candidate. Continue only against relevant external observations; the ten crafted starting programs limit generalization.

  • W071 Why Are Agentic Pull Requests Merged or Rejected? An Empirical Study

    Different rejection causes inform deciding whether another implementation attempt is justified or a workflow decision is missing. Inferred and unspecified PR explanations cannot be treated as confirmed repair diagnostics, and shared AIDev records remain dependent.

  • W226 Large-Scale Study of GitHub Copilot Trajectories
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Recorded feedback-loop timing informs retaining the diagnostic and intervention history before another attempt. Non-random intervention and task difficulty prevent interpreting loop counts as proof that retries are effective or autonomous continuation is safe.

  • W229 Your Wish Is My Commit: Over-Compliant Refactoring in AI Coding Agents
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Continued edits to an already-clean codebase caution against equating more attempts or a completion declaration with justified progress. The deliberate repeated-refactoring stress test does not estimate ordinary development churn.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Replace indefinite regeneration with a sequence of explainable repairs whose eligibility can be checked by someone outside the maker.

When to use it

  • A test, reproduction or concrete review finding identifies an in-scope defect.
  • The next attempt has a plausible targeted remedy and sufficient remaining budget.

When to avoid it

  • The only feedback is that the answer is unsatisfactory, with no actionable observation.
  • The disagreement concerns intended behavior, unavailable authority or a prohibited operation.

Before you start

  • A persistent task and attempt record with explicit budgets and exits.
  • An oracle or other evidence source that the maker cannot rewrite to achieve a pass.

How to apply it

  1. Capture the failed obligation, exact candidate, diagnostic and relevant environment before proposing another attempt.
  2. Decide whether the failure is repairable within the current contract or needs a named owner to clarify scope.
  3. State the narrow change expected to address the diagnostic and check that it is permitted and affordable.
  4. Apply the repair, rerun the protected check and examine relevant regressions for unintended effects.
  5. Continue only if new evidence supports another eligible attempt; otherwise retain the history and stop as review-ready, exhausted, blocked or escalated.

Illustrative example

A checker shows that a revised export drops one allowed status value. The maker corrects that mapping and reruns the status cases. The next review raises an unresolved question about whether that status should exist for a different customer class. This is no longer a mechanical retry: the task stops for a requirement decision, preserving the previous failure and the repaired candidate.

What to check

  • Each retry names both the prior diagnostic and the remedy it is testing.
  • The objective, protected expectation and cumulative budget remain intact across attempts.
  • The exit explains whether evidence is sufficient for review or which unresolved issue prevents further action.

Expected outputs

  • Attempt ledger linking diagnostics, remedies, candidates and results.
  • Review-ready evidence or an explicit stop with the required next decision.

Risks and failure modes

  • An agent can overfit a visible failure while missing adjacent behavior.
  • Repeated rejection without useful diagnostics can consume resources and encourage unauthorized changes to the success criterion.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:027PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Maker–Checker: Separate Production from Acceptance

Family. Tests, Oracles and Acceptance Evidence

Separate the responsibility for producing a candidate from the responsibility for checking its claims, while protecting the approved objective and expected results from both inappropriate edits and self-approval. Evaluate independence through the origin of expectations, available evidence and effective permissions. Two roles or two models can still share the same mistake and cannot replace accountable acceptance.

26 linked sources · 21 external sources · 5 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (26)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

26 linked sources shown

Polimi (10)

  • W072 AI-to-AI Code Reviews of GitHub Pull Requests
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Agent-on-agent review demonstrates role separation without demonstrating independent error detection. Rare distinct actor pairs and unmeasured quality prevent treating automation density as evidence that the maker-checker arrangement works.

  • W075 Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    A self-correction disadvantage outside programming cautions against assuming the maker will reliably detect its own mistakes. Transfer to code checking remains a hypothesis; the benchmark does not validate a software maker-checker workflow.

  • W078 Beyond the Surface: Measuring Self-Preference in LLM Judgments
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Model and training-data similarity can bias judgments, so assigning a nominally separate checker does not establish independent evidence. The text-judgment setting does not quantify the same effect in code review.

  • W079 Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Shared errors across models caution against equating a second model with an independent oracle. Preserve independent expectations and checks; general LLM datasets do not predict which errors a particular coding pair will share.

  • W082 LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Preference for a model's own generations challenges the assumption that self-grading supplies a meaningful independent check. The evidence concerns summarization, so the mapping identifies an independence risk rather than a measured code-review effect.

  • W084 Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Preference for familiar output styles cautions against accepting a judge's favorable score as independent quality evidence. These dialogue judgments do not establish production-software error rates or validate a remedy.

  • W101 Articulate but Wrong: Self-Review Failures in LLM-Based Code Modernization
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Models' failure to spot semantic changes in their own ports cautions against using self-review as independent checking. Fluent explanation of a migration rule does not establish behavioral preservation, and the small traps limit generalization.

  • W102 Cross-Model LLM Code Review: Should You Use Claude to Review Codex or Vice Versa?
    Evaluates a practice component · primary reading for this source

    The narrow benchmark evaluates a second model reviewing another model's implementation and finds order-dependent benefits and harm. It tests that checker configuration, not independent oracles, protected permissions, or the full acceptance workflow.

    Evaluated component: Using a second model to review another model's implementation under the benchmark's tested model orderings.

  • W108 Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Persistent acceptance of a model's own wrong answers means genuine average quality differences do not eliminate self-review bias. The MBPP+ benchmark limits inference to that setting rather than production PR acceptance.

  • W212 Software Engineering in the Age of Delegation
    Illustrates practice

    Independent implementations and cross-team testing illustrate separating production from a subsequent check in a teaching design. The report does not establish independent error detection, protected permissions or the efficacy of the full maker-checker workflow.

  • O033 The "Trust, But Verify" Pattern For AI-Assisted Engineering

    Requiring a justified check for each AI-produced change informs the evidence the checker must obtain before acceptance. The practitioner argument does not make a generated check independent merely because it exists.

  • O051 Agentic Verification
    Cautions about practice

Pragmatic Engineer (4)

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Give a candidate a meaningful opportunity to fail against evidence the maker did not define merely by observing its own output.

When to use it

  • A wrong-but-green candidate would have a material consequence or be difficult for a reviewer to spot.
  • The workflow can separate candidate production, independent findings and final acceptance authority.

When to avoid it

  • The checker simply repeats the maker's explanation or uses expectations generated from the candidate.
  • A second role adds ceremony while the maker can still rewrite the protected oracle.

Before you start

  • Expected behavior derived from an authorized source with a protected revision.
  • Distinct effective permissions and result channels for maker, checker and acceptance owner.

How to apply it

  1. Define what the maker may change and exclude the approved contract and protected expected results from its write scope.
  2. Give the checker the actual candidate, relevant authority and independently justified cases rather than only the maker's summary.
  3. Have the checker seek discrepancies and report reproducible findings with locators, assumptions and uncertainty.
  4. Return confirmed in-scope failures as bounded repair requests; send ambiguous requirements to their owner.
  5. Present the renewed candidate and current evidence to the accountable reviewer, preserving the distinction between checked and accepted.

Illustrative example

The maker changes how stored decisions replay. A checker runs an independently specified case requiring the original response to survive a policy update. It reports a concrete mismatch but cannot edit the candidate. The maker repairs the implementation without changing that expectation. The final reviewer inspects current results and decides whether the candidate can advance; no checker status alone grants release approval.

What to check

  • The expected answer has an origin independent of the candidate's observed output.
  • Neither role can silently alter protected authority or convert its own claim into acceptance.
  • A known wrong candidate is rejected, and evidence is renewed after a relevant repair.

Expected outputs

  • Role and permission map plus independently grounded findings.
  • Candidate-bound evidence and a separate acceptance disposition.

Risks and failure modes

  • Different model names can mask shared context gaps or the same faulty requirement.
  • A read-only checker cannot protect an expectation that the maker remains able to edit.

PAT:028PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Skills and Context Engineering: Remove Intent Debt

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Package recurring work instructions as a maintained, versioned skill or context aid with an owner, applicability and source references. Separate procedural guidance from retrieved evidence, task state and tool permissions. The aim is to make missing or ambiguous intent visible and reduce repeated clarification where justified, without claiming that a larger instruction file removes all intent debt.

9 linked sources · 4 external sources · 5 book records. Read the associations ↓

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make recurring procedural knowledge reusable while preserving a clear path to the current authorized objective and its unresolved questions.

When to use it

  • A repeated task has stable procedural steps that workers otherwise reconstruct inconsistently.
  • Recurring misunderstandings can be traced to omitted context or unclear precedence.

When to avoid it

  • A one-off instruction would be generalized without evidence of reuse.
  • The proposed skill mixes tool credentials, authority decisions and unverified repository claims into one trusted block.

Before you start

  • A named maintainer and a versioned source for the procedure.
  • Applicability conditions, required inputs, expected outputs and independently enforced permission boundaries.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the recurring failure and write only the procedural guidance needed to address it.
  2. State scope, input requirements, evidence requirements and stop conditions, linking authoritative sources instead of copying mutable rules everywhere.
  3. Version and review the guidance, separating stable instructions from task-specific state and retrieved material.
  4. At use time, verify applicability and freshness against the current task and permissions; keep unresolved intent visible.
  5. Record concrete failures or maintenance changes, then revise or retire the skill when it no longer provides useful guidance.

Illustrative example

A team writes a release-note drafting skill that requires a defined revision range, source links and explicit exclusions. The skill explains the workflow but grants no publishing access and contains no permanent claim about which features are released. Each run obtains its current approved inputs. When the release process changes, the owner updates the version and records which old instructions should no longer be used.

What to check

  • The skill identifies its owner, version, applicable tasks and renewal triggers.
  • A worker can distinguish procedural advice from evidence and authoritative decisions.
  • A useful trial checks the actual deliverable and exposes missing context rather than merely confirming the skill file was loaded.

Expected outputs

  • Versioned, owned procedural guidance with source links.
  • Applicability and renewal record from actual uses.

Risks and failure modes

  • Accumulated instructions can conflict or crowd out the evidence needed for the present task.
  • An apparently official skill can launder an old assumption into a current requirement unless its authority and scope are checked.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

Memory and Retrieval: Read What the Model Could Not Know

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Retrieve task-relevant information that is absent from the model's immediate context, preserving source, revision, validity and authority. Memory can contain past actions, semantic summaries, instructions or approved decisions, and those types are not interchangeable. A useful system can abstain when evidence is missing or conflicting instead of turning retrieved plausibility into approved knowledge.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Ground a task in the information it actually needs while keeping uncertainty and conflicting sources available for review.

When to use it

  • Repository-specific decisions, recent changes or task history are needed to answer the next question.
  • A long-running task needs selective access to evidence beyond a compact resume record.

When to avoid it

  • The system treats the top-ranked passage as authoritative without checking its provenance.
  • A missing decision is being filled by a plausible historical analogy instead of being raised with its owner.

Before you start

  • Source records with stable locators, revisions and validity scopes.
  • A distinction between instructions, evidence, task state and authoritative decisions.

How to apply it

  1. Define the information need and the type of claim required: observation, current rule, past event or procedural instruction.
  2. Retrieve candidate sources and retain their identities, scope and dates or versions relevant to the task.
  3. Check applicability and authority, consulting original records when a derived summary cannot resolve a consequential claim.
  4. Present supported facts separately from inferences, conflicts and omissions; abstain on unresolved questions that affect acceptance.
  5. Bind useful retrieved evidence to the task record and set renewal triggers for any derived memory reused later.

Illustrative example

A resumed agent finds two cards describing different policy thresholds. It checks the source revisions and discovers that one governs historical decisions while the other governs new requests. It retrieves the approved delta and preserves both scoped facts. If the relevant approval record is unavailable, it reports that gap instead of choosing the newer-looking card as authority.

What to check

  • Material claims can be traced from a summary back to the source used.
  • Current applicability and authority are checked independently of retrieval rank or recency.
  • Missing or contradictory evidence produces an explicit uncertainty or owner question rather than a fabricated answer.

Expected outputs

  • Task-specific evidence set with provenance and applicability.
  • Derived memory or answer that distinguishes supported claims, inference and unresolved gaps.

Risks and failure modes

  • Retrieved instructions embedded in untrusted material can attempt to cross the tool-permission boundary.
  • A compressed memory card may omit the qualifier that determines whether a fact applies to the present task.

PAT:030PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Connectors and Tools: Move Exact Work Outside the Weights

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Delegate exact retrieval, computation or controlled operations to tools whose interfaces and outputs can be checked. The model selects or explains work while the executor performs the specified operation within an enforced permission envelope. Deterministic arithmetic or successful API execution establishes only that operation's result; it does not authorize the external effect or validate the task's underlying assumptions.
