Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Give a reviewer enough context to diagnose whether a particular intended change has been achieved.

When to use it

  • A proposed patch contains multiple unrelated outcomes or failures are difficult to attribute.
  • An agent needs an item that fits the available evidence, review capacity, and execution budget.

When to avoid it

  • Splitting would temporarily violate an invariant that must change atomically across several components.

Before you start

  • The intended outcome and affected interfaces are understood.
  • Relevant checks and required integration obligations are identifiable.

How to apply it

  1. State the behavioral outcome in one sentence and identify what remains explicitly outside the item.
  2. Trace the dependencies required to make that outcome coherent; include necessary files even when this enlarges the diff.
  3. Choose a focused acceptance check and the regressions that protect neighboring obligations.
  4. Implement and inspect the increment as a unit, recording any newly discovered dependency or ambiguity.
  5. Return an independently reviewable result; create a separate item for unrelated findings instead of broadening the current one.

Illustrative example

Changing how historical requests are replayed touches a handler, storage adapter, and contract test. Those files belong to one verifiable behavior and stay together. A nearby formatting cleanup and a new reporting endpoint become separate items. If a regression fails, the reviewer can relate it to replay semantics instead of reconstructing three unrelated changes.

What to check

  • The item has one explainable acceptance question and a traceable result.
  • Its boundaries include the dependencies necessary to preserve the relevant invariant.
  • The proposed split leaves a viable integration path and records remaining work.

Expected outputs

  • A scoped work item with acceptance and regression checks.
  • A reviewable candidate and separate follow-up items.

Risks and failure modes

  • Using file count as a proxy for simplicity can split behavior across incompatible changes.
  • Local passes can conceal an integration failure when each chunk is checked in isolation.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:047PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Context Engineering

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Assemble the minimum relevant context while preserving the distinction between instructions, retrieved information, task state, and authorized evidence. Give each item a role, version, source, and validity scope. This helps an assistant reason from the right material without treating a plausible retrieved passage or an old checkpoint as current decision authority.

8 linked sources · 7 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Reduce mistakes caused by missing system knowledge, conflicting context roles, or stale information presented without qualification.

When to use it

  • A brownfield task depends on repository conventions, historical rationale, or external decisions.
  • Long sessions repeatedly lose important constraints or accumulate irrelevant retrieved material.

When to avoid it

  • The real blocker is an absent policy decision; supplying more context cannot create the missing authority.

Before you start

  • A task envelope identifies the decision and permissible actions.
  • Source locators, versions, and knowledge owners are available where material.

How to apply it

  1. List what must be known to perform and check the task, separating obligations from background explanation.
  2. Retrieve specific passages or artifacts with their locators and revision scope rather than indiscriminately copying entire collections.
  3. Label authoritative decisions, observations, tentative inferences, and historical records so their roles remain visible.
  4. Create a concise working state containing the current objective, evidence, open questions, and next permitted action.
  5. Refresh affected context after a relevant change; retain obsolete records as history while excluding them from current authority.

Illustrative example

An agent repairing a replay endpoint receives the current contract, a historical policy note, a storage map, and the last failed check. The historical note explains an old response but cannot authorize behavior for new requests. The context bundle makes that distinction explicit, preventing the assistant from applying yesterday’s threshold simply because it is well documented.

What to check

  • Material claims link to identifiable sources and validity scopes.
  • The bundle separates approved instructions from retrieved or inferred information.
  • A changed rule triggers refresh of the affected task state and dependencies.

Expected outputs

  • A typed, task-specific context bundle.
  • A record of unresolved questions and refresh triggers.

Risks and failure modes

  • Context stuffing can bury the deciding constraint beneath relevant-looking detail.
  • Repository prose or retrieved content can be mistaken for operational instructions.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:072 · Handoff Chain

PAT:048PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

The Explainability Test

Family. Competence, Learning and Mentoring

Ask a developer to reconstruct how a candidate works, why its invariants hold, and where it could fail. Evaluate that explanation as a comprehension task using concrete predictions and evidence. A clear explanation can expose missing understanding, but persuasive language, whether produced by a person or an assistant, is insufficient proof that the implementation is correct.

21 linked sources · 20 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (21)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

21 linked sources shown

Polimi (15)

  • W090 Decoding the Representation of Code in the Brain: An fMRI Study of Code Review and Expertise
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Neural classification of review activity cannot establish that a developer understands a candidate or reviews it effectively. Keep observable prediction and explanation tasks separate from physiological proxies, with no production-effectiveness inference.

  • W113 I Would Have Written My Code Differently: Beginners Struggle to Understand LLM-Generated Code
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Novices' difficulty judging whether generated programs meet stated intent motivates concrete prediction and explanation tasks when checking understanding. The short introductory Python setting does not prove the effectiveness of the explainability practice for professionals.

  • W114 Correlates of programmer efficacy and their link to experience: a combined EEG and eye-tracking study
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Associations between selective reading, engagement and efficacy inform assessing demonstrated reasoning instead of relying only on years of experience. The thirty-seven-programmer correlation does not validate a teaching or comprehension intervention.

  • W122 AI Didn't Make Programming Easier. It Just Made It Differently Difficult
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The argument that effort moves toward mental models and judgment informs asking developers to explain consequential behavior instead of equating generated syntax with understanding. It is a thought piece, not a measured shift or tested comprehension method.

  • W154 Comprehension Debt in GenAI-Assisted Software Engineering Projects
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Student reports of latent understanding gaps motivate checking whether a developer can explain a generated candidate and predict its behavior. The diary study lacks an objective comprehension baseline and does not validate the explanation test itself.

  • W162 40 Years of Designing Code Comprehension Experiments: A Systematic Mapping Study
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The lack of personally authored code in many comprehension experiments makes authorship and familiarity relevant conditions for a comprehension check. The pre-AI mapping study does not validate an agent-assisted explanation intervention.

  • W164 Program Comprehension and Code Complexity Metrics: An fMRI Study
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The partial relationship between complexity metrics and cognitive effort informs assessing actual reasoning rather than substituting a complexity score. Vocabulary and text size can affect the task; artificial snippets and nineteen participants limit transfer.

  • W166 Comprehension of computer code relies primarily on domain-general executive brain regions
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The distinction between code comprehension and ordinary language processing informs using code-specific predictions and explanations when examining understanding. Small-program psychology does not establish codebase ownership, correctness or the efficacy of this assessment workflow.

  • W169 Simultaneous Measurement of Program Comprehension with fMRI and Eye Tracking: A Case Study
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Signal and measurement limits of fMRI and eye tracking caution against using instrumentation as proof that a developer understands code. This feasibility work does not test an AI intervention or validate the explainability workflow.

  • W172 Measuring neural efficiency of program comprehension
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The role of informative naming identifies a condition that can influence performance on a code-comprehension task. Reduced cognitive effort in a small trained sample does not establish correct explanations, learning retention or full-project understanding.

  • W179 A systematic literature review on the usage of eye-tracking in software engineering
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Uncontrolled own-code versus others' code familiarity is a design issue when choosing a comprehension assessment. The pre-LLM review identifies a study-design gap, not an outcome showing that an explanation task improves understanding.

  • W181 Understanding understanding source code with functional magnetic resonance imaging
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The distinction between comprehension and syntax spotting informs choosing an assessment that requires behavioral prediction rather than superficial recognition. Contrived snippets with obscured names do not validate the full explanation workflow for maintained systems.

  • W190 How do Humans and LLMs Process Confusing Code?
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Correlated human confusion and model perplexity suggest candidate code locations for a concrete comprehension challenge. A reused small EEG dataset and one model do not establish general human understanding or validate perplexity as its substitute.

  • W211 The Effects of GitHub Copilot on Computing Students’ Programming Effectiveness, Efficiency, and Processes in Brownfield Programming Tasks
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Improved tested progress alongside understanding concerns motivates checking a learner's explanation independently of task completion. Ten undergraduates on an unfamiliar application do not establish professional comprehension gains or the effectiveness of the explanation practice.

  • W227 Can VIBE Drive Development? Threats and Opportunities
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The opinion's explicit human-comprehension requirement informs asking developers to explain generated behavior before relying on it. This is proposed guidance with historical analogies, not an empirical validation of the explanation test or a new quantitative study.

Osmani (2)

  • O017 The 80% Problem in Agentic Coding
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Comprehension debt despite increased shipping makes reconstruction of behavior and failure modes a separate acceptance concern. The illustrative 80% framing cannot quantify the prevalence of weak developer understanding.

  • O023 Treat AI-Generated code as a draft
    Informs practice

    Responsible understanding before merge informs asking the maintainer to explain the candidate's behavior and potential failures. An explanation is a comprehension check, not proof that the generated implementation is correct.

Pragmatic Engineer (1)

  • P069 Comparing interviews at 8 large tech companies
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The emphasis on systems-design assessment informs asking an engineer to expose reasoning about system behavior rather than judging only output. The source follows one pseudonymous candidate across companies; it does not validate an explainability test or represent independent samples of candidates.

Fowler website (2)

  • F019 I still care about the code
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Responsibility for operational code informs requiring a maintainer to understand behavior and possible failures rather than accepting generated output on fluency alone. The professional position is not a calibrated universal threshold for review depth.

  • F024 Assessing internal quality while coding with an agent
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    Erik Doernenburg's expert inspection illustrates reconstructing the intended type model and identifying duplication or unnecessary mechanisms that compilation misses. The anecdote does not establish a population-level quality effect or make an explanation a complete correctness proof.

This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:NDSE:06

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Check whether the person expected to maintain or review a change has a usable mental model of its behavior.

When to use it

  • A developer adopts generated code they did not substantially construct themselves.
  • A handoff or review depends on understanding an invariant, failure path, or design tradeoff.

When to avoid it

  • The only goal is to prove correctness; use independent tests and other appropriate evidence as well.

Before you start

  • A bounded candidate and a relevant behavioral contract.
  • Questions with observable answers and a reviewer who can assess the reasoning.

How to apply it

  1. Select a consequential path or invariant rather than asking for a general code tour.
  2. Ask the learner to predict a concrete outcome before running the program or consulting an assistant.
  3. Require a walkthrough connecting the prediction to specific code, data, and authorized behavior.
  4. Introduce a counterexample or small variation and ask what must change, what remains stable, and why.
  5. Compare the explanation with execution evidence, record misconceptions, and give a targeted follow-up task.

Illustrative example

After accepting an AI-assisted storage refactor, a maintainer predicts what a repeated request returns after a policy update. They trace the lookup key, stored response, and conflict path before observing the run. If the explanation depends on reevaluating current policy, the reviewer has found a comprehension gap even when the existing regression suite happens to pass.

What to check

  • The learner predicts behavior on an unseen variation, not just the demonstrated example.
  • Claims about code paths and invariants withstand inspection and relevant execution.
  • Misconceptions lead to a corrective exercise whose result is assessed separately.

Expected outputs

  • A short comprehension assessment with observed gaps.
  • A targeted explanation, repair, or transfer exercise.

Risks and failure modes

  • A fluent assistant-written answer can substitute for the learner’s own reconstruction.
  • Confidence or presentation quality can bias assessment away from the actual reasoning.

  • Developer Learning, Mentoring and Comprehension Debt — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:049PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Runtime-in-the-Loop

Family. Architecture, Evolution and Maintenance

Bring observed execution into a development decision by connecting a runtime question to an expected result, a controlled scenario, and the candidate that was run. Use logs, traces, or measurements to resolve that question. Record conditions and limitations so a successful local observation is not presented as an unperformed production or performance evaluation.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Replace speculative reasoning about an exercised path with inspectable observations that affect the next engineering decision.

When to use it

  • A behavior depends on state, integration, ordering, or runtime configuration that static reading leaves uncertain.
  • An architectural change needs evidence that a relevant behavior survives the new representation.

When to avoid it

  • The required experiment would cause unauthorized external effects or cannot produce a trustworthy observation.

Before you start

  • An explicit question, expected behavior, and safe execution environment.
  • A known candidate version and instruments appropriate to the question.

How to apply it

  1. State the claim to examine and define the input, initial state, and expected observation before execution.
  2. Record the candidate, configuration, data, command, and relevant environmental assumptions.
  3. Run the scenario and capture the raw observation without replacing unexpected results with the intended story.
  4. Compare observations with the expectation; classify a mismatch as a candidate defect, environment issue, or unresolved requirement.
  5. Use the diagnosis to choose a bounded repair or further experiment, retaining both positive and negative results.

Illustrative example

A representation migration appears to preserve request replay. The team starts with a stored response from the earlier policy, restarts the service with the new representation, and repeats the request. The captured response and storage trace answer the replay question. They do not establish throughput under load, recovery from every failure, or behavior on a different deployment configuration.

What to check

  • The reported result can be traced to a real invocation and candidate snapshot.
  • The observation tests the stated expectation rather than a convenient substitute.
  • Unmeasured claims and environmental differences remain explicit in the decision.

Expected outputs

  • A reproducible scenario and captured runtime evidence.
  • A bounded conclusion with the resulting engineering action.

Risks and failure modes

  • Instrumentation may miss the deciding event or alter the behavior under examination.
  • A familiar local setup can encourage unjustified claims about operational performance.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Quality, Architecture and Maintainability — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:050PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Learning Loop Preservation

Family. Competence, Learning and Mentoring

Preserve opportunities to predict, diagnose, explain, and repair while using AI assistance. Define the capability a learner should retain, design tasks that require their own reasoning, and assess transfer separately from immediate completion. Assistance can remain available, but its output must not be mistaken for evidence that the learner can perform the same judgment independently.

21 linked sources · 17 external sources · 4 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (21)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

21 linked sources shown

Polimi (8)

  • W015 Agentic Delegation and the Language Frontier of Software Developers: A Model and Evidence from Claude Code on GitHub
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Contributions across more languages can show assisted reach without retained proficiency. Learning assessment should use independent reasoning and transfer tasks; repository breadth alone cannot demonstrate that developers learned the underlying languages.

  • W116 Using Biometrics to Understand AI-Assisted Coding Performance and its Perception
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Apparent generation progress alongside possible reduced engagement cautions against equating assisted completion with learning. Student writing tasks and uncertain physiological endpoints cannot establish retained programming competence or long-term skill loss.

  • W117 The Augmentation Trap: AI Productivity and the Cost of Cognitive Offloading
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The proposed incentive mechanism motivates preserving opportunities to acquire knowledge during assisted work. It is a theoretical reason to examine learning, not longitudinal evidence that the expanded learning-loop practice prevents delayed productivity costs.

  • W118 How AI Impacts Skill Formation
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The immediate learning quiz cannot establish delayed retention or long-run professional performance. Preserve unaided conceptual assessment while treating the unresolved percentage normalization as a reason to avoid a numerical effect claim for this practice.

  • W119 Training in the Age of AI: A Theory of Career Viability
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The apprenticeship model motivates retaining junior opportunities to practice consequential reasoning rather than automating all developmental work. Its labor-pipeline prediction is not an observed effect or a validated learning-preservation intervention.

  • W121 Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Essay-writing engagement and recall findings cannot establish programming skill loss or the efficacy of a learning-preservation workflow. Their contested interpretation makes direct transfer to developer retention an explicit evidence gap.

  • W212 Software Engineering in the Age of Delegation
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    The course's oral examinations, modeling and independent work illustrate designing assisted development around retained human judgment. Preliminary reports and instructor observations do not establish comparative learning benefit or long-term capability.

  • W214 AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Immediate unassisted performance after brief help on non-programming tasks cannot establish durable developer skill loss. It motivates separating assisted success from independent assessment, without claiming that the expanded learning-preservation workflow was tested.

Osmani (5)

  • O003 Agentic Skill Decay
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The skill-decay argument identifies reasoning, debugging and comprehension as activities that must remain available when implementation is delegated. It motivates a learning-preservation boundary, without supplying a measured rate of developer skill loss.

  • O035 AI Won't Kill Junior Devs - But Your Hiring Strategy Might

  • O036 Avoiding Skill Atrophy in the Age of AI
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Avoiding every difficult step removes reasoning practice needed to supervise later output, directly identifying a boundary for learning-preserving assistance. The interpretation does not quantify retained-skill loss.

  • O057 Don't Outsource the Learning
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Forming hypotheses, requesting explanations and periodically reconstructing solutions unaided inform preserving independent reasoning within assisted work. The mixed-population research synthesis does not establish long-term causal skill loss among developers.

  • O062 Earning taste and judgment
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Unaided implementation, deliberate code reading and separate specification/verification practice inform preserving the reasoning that routine delegation can remove. The guidance does not constitute a controlled learning intervention or a new employment estimate.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep successful assisted delivery from concealing an inability to understand or maintain the resulting system.

When to use it

  • Repeated automation removes the debugging or design decisions through which a developer normally learns.
  • A mentoring program must distinguish supported performance from retained individual capability.

When to avoid it

  • The activity has no learning objective and adding a training exercise would interfere with a time-critical authorized response.

Before you start

  • A specific skill target and a suitably bounded exercise.
  • A mentor or assessment method that can evaluate reasoning and provide feedback.

How to apply it

  1. Choose the capability to retain, such as diagnosing replay errors, and define observable evidence of that capability.
  2. Ask for a prediction or initial diagnosis before revealing a generated solution or explanation.
  3. Use assistance for targeted feedback, alternative hypotheses, or scaffolding while keeping consequential reasoning with the learner.
  4. Have the learner repair or explain the result in their own terms and identify why rejected approaches fail.
  5. Assess a different case later, recording available assistance and distinguishing retention from repeated familiarity with the original example.

Illustrative example

A junior engineer first predicts why a stored request behaves differently after a policy change, then compares the prediction with a trace. An assistant offers focused questions rather than the completed patch. After the repair, the mentor assigns a different historical-data case at a later session. The second result informs a learning judgment; the first task’s green tests alone do not.

What to check

  • The learner performs a meaningful reasoning step before seeing the proposed answer.
  • Assessment separates task completion, explanation quality, and later transfer.
  • Observed misconceptions change the next exercise rather than disappearing into a completion score.

Expected outputs

  • A capability objective and assisted-practice plan.
  • Separate records of immediate performance and transfer observations.

Risks and failure modes

  • Removing all assistance can turn a learning exercise into avoidable frustration rather than useful practice.
  • Reusing the same example can reward memorization and overstate transferable understanding.

PAT:051PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Security-First Development

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Examine security concerns before generating or adopting a change, treating the product and the agent’s development environment as separate attack surfaces. Translate consequential threats into concrete controls and checks, then carry findings into the release decision. Early attention organizes the work; it does not make a secure outcome follow automatically from the practice’s name.

15 linked sources · 13 external sources · 2 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (15)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

15 linked sources shown

Polimi (13)

  • W032 Understanding the Impact of AI Code Assistants on Security API Usage
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Functional correctness without reliable secure API use cautions against treating successful implementation as sufficient security evidence. Preserve checks for the relevant security behavior; the forty-four-participant result does not establish all API or developer risks.

  • W035 Security in the Age of AI Teammates: An Empirical Study of Agentic Pull Requests on GitHub
    Informs practice

    Separating hardening from vulnerability repair informs naming the security obligation before assessing a change. A hardening label or accepted PR does not demonstrate that a vulnerability was fixed; shared AIDev observations remain dependent.

  • W039 Human-Written vs. AI-Generated Code: A Large-Scale Study of Defects, Vulnerabilities, and Complexity
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Different observed fault types inform selecting security checks for the actual generated candidate instead of applying a universal human-versus-AI quality ranking. Authorship attribution and sampling bound the relevance of the reported vulnerabilities.

  • W040 Security Weaknesses of Copilot-Generated Code in GitHub Projects: An Empirical Study
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The selected snippets' security warnings motivate targeted security inspection and checked remediation. Static findings and partial repairs do not establish complete security or an AI-versus-human difference without a comparable control.

  • W041 Security Vulnerabilities in AI-Generated Code: A Large-Scale Analysis of Public GitHub Repositories
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Language-dependent vulnerability observations inform tailoring threat checks to the candidate's language and use. Marker-based sampling and the absence of a matched human baseline prevent a general security hierarchy or prevalence claim.

  • W042 Security Degradation in Iterative AI Code Generation: A Systematic Analysis of the Paradox
    Informs practice

    Security degradation during iteration makes security obligations relevant to each changed candidate, even when the stated goal is improvement. The study motivates external checks but does not establish a universally effective security gate.

  • W045 Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking Vulnerability of Agent-Generated Code in Real-World Tasks
    Informs practice

    Separate functional and security criteria inform defining security-specific obligations before accepting generated features. The benchmark tests agents on selected requests, not the efficacy of the expanded security-first workflow.

  • W047 Lost at C: A User Study on the Security Implications of Large Language Model Code Assistants
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Similar bug rates in one linked-list task cannot establish that assistance is generally security-neutral or negate different studies. Security decisions must retain the particular language, task and assessed failure modes.

  • W048 Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Vulnerable results from deliberately sensitive prompts motivate negative cases for named security threats. The curated 2021-model scenarios do not quantify present-day vulnerability prevalence or validate a complete secure-development process.

  • W061 2025 GenAI Code Security Report
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Functional model improvements without corresponding security-test gains caution against treating general model progress as security assurance. The vendor-created benchmark supports only its selected prompts and assessed failure modes.

  • W062 Vibe Security Radar
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Field disclosures with coding-agent provenance supply concrete failures for considering relevant threat checks. Incomplete provenance coverage and an uninterpretable denominator prevent estimating general application risk or the effectiveness of a security workflow.

  • W067 (Don't) Trust, but (Don't) Verify: Developers' Attention to Security in AI-Generated Code
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Selection of unsafe suggestions cautions against relying on ordinary user acceptance as a security check. The association between editing and fewer vulnerabilities is not causal proof of an effective control and concerns four C tasks.

  • W203 Generation and Verification: Human-Agent Collaboration for Safety-Critical Automotive Software Engineering
    Cautions about practice

    Pattern-based conformance indicators cannot certify functional safety or complete standards compliance. Keep the exact security and safety obligations separate from what the industrial pilot's checks actually observed.

NDSE2 chapters (1)

  • NDSE2:C06 Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The chapter threat-models both the generated application and the agent runtime. It informs security-first development with enforceable permissions and security evidence tied to the release decision.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent a functionally correct candidate from obscuring an unmanaged application threat or an overpowered development tool.

When to use it

  • A change handles sensitive information, authorization, external input, or consequential operations.
  • An assistant gains tools, dependencies, credentials, or access to a repository containing untrusted material.

When to avoid it

  • A generic checklist would replace an already required specialist review of a consequential threat.

Before you start

  • An inventory of protected assets and permitted operations.
  • Owners for application security, tool permissions, and unresolved exceptions.

How to apply it

  1. Identify what the resulting application must protect and which attacker-controlled inputs could reach it.
  2. Separately map what the development agent can read, write, invoke, and transmit through its available tools.
  3. Choose controls tied to named threats, keeping authority and sensitive expectations outside the maker’s writable scope.
  4. Exercise relevant negative cases and denial paths; record scanner findings as signals requiring interpretation.
  5. Carry unresolved threats, applied controls, and residual uncertainty into the accountable review and release process.

Illustrative example

An assistant adds a request-import feature. Product checks examine malformed input and whether users can import data outside their entitlement. Development controls separately prevent the assistant from sending fixture data to an arbitrary endpoint or altering protected acceptance rules. Passing parser tests answers neither of those permission questions, so the evidence record keeps both surfaces visible.

What to check

  • Material threats have an explicit control, test, or recorded unresolved decision.
  • Denied tool operations are enforced by the environment, not only by prompt instructions.
  • The acceptance record distinguishes functional results from security findings and permissions.

Expected outputs

  • Two scoped threat assessments and their control mapping.
  • Security evidence and unresolved issues for review.

Risks and failure modes

  • A clean scanner report can be mistaken for a complete threat assessment.
  • A secure application candidate can still be produced through an uncontrolled tool or data boundary.

PAT:052PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Review Gauntlet

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Route review effort according to the change’s impact, uncertainty, and available reviewer capacity. Select the checks and people needed to answer its consequential questions, preserve actionable findings, and finish with an accountable verdict. The gauntlet is a configurable review path; imposing the same sequence on every patch can create delay without proportionate information.

36 linked sources · 33 external sources · 3 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (36)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

36 linked sources shown

Polimi (23)

  • W021 The AI Engineering Report 2026: The Acceleration Whiplash
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The association between increased throughput and slower review makes reviewer capacity a concrete admission constraint to examine. The commercial observational record does not show that a particular review sequence improves safety or throughput.

  • W034 Comparing AI Coding Agents: A Task-Stratified Analysis of Pull Request Acceptance
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Task-sensitive acceptance informs routing review by the nature of the change rather than an agent's aggregate reputation. Maintainer acceptance is not verified quality, and the shared dataset limits independent corroboration.

  • W035 Security in the Age of AI Teammates: An Empirical Study of Agentic Pull Requests on GitHub
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Long security reviews and sensitivity to PR complexity inform allocating review capacity and expertise to consequential changes. The observational findings do not establish an optimal review path or a causal complexity threshold.

  • W036 On the Use of Agentic Coding: An Empirical Study of Pull Requests on GitHub
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Frequent human revision of merged agent changes makes review and rework part of the delivery process. Merge rates alone cannot establish reliability or justify removing the responsible review decision in a small adoption cohort.

  • W063 An Endless Stream of AI Slop: How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Contributor accounts of generation outpacing review inform limiting admission to available maintainer capacity. They identify a workflow concern, but forum perceptions do not quantify review costs or establish that a particular review route works.

  • W065 These Aren't the Reviews You're Looking For: How Humans Review AI-Generated Pull Requests
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Recorded GitHub reviews do not capture all review rigor, so absent events cannot establish that acceptance was unexamined. Preserve this observability limit when using review records to route work or judge scrutiny.

  • W068 Behind Agentic Pull Requests: An Empirical Study on Developer Interventions in AI Agent-Authored Pull Requests
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Less frequent but more extensive interventions inform accounting for review effort and guidance, not merely counting touched PRs. Metadata events and the shared AIDev cohort do not certify actual review quality.

  • W069 Same Scrutiny, More Time: Eye Tracking Insights into Reviewing LLM-Labelled Code
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Longer fixation on AI-labelled code cannot establish improved defect detection when injected-defect detection was not assessed. Treat attention time as a review burden measure, not evidence that a label-based review route is effective.

  • W073 The Effect of Complexity and Provenance on Code Review Decisions: Evidence from a Controlled Experiment
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Reviewers' increased acceptance of wrong complex changes makes complexity a concrete review-routing concern. Controlled decisions support examining that burden, not a production incident estimate or a universally effective review sequence.

  • W081 Deep Learning-based Code Reviews: A Paradigm Shift or a Double-Edged Sword?
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Extra time spent starting from LLM comments without finding more major seeded defects cautions against adding review stages by default. The small one-system study does not establish a universal cost or failure of assisted review.

  • W083 A Study on Developer Behaviors for Validating and Repairing LLM-Generated Code Using Eye Tracking and IDE Actions
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The small experiment shows that provenance disclosure can change active validation and repair, informing how a reviewer is briefed. It does not establish that labels alone improve every review process or reconcile all passive-label studies.

  • W091 Automation bias and verification complexity: a systematic review
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Greater bias when suggestions are difficult to verify makes checkability a relevant factor in selecting a review path. The synthesis is not directly about code and does not establish an effective software-review configuration.

  • W093 Automating Low-Risk Code Review at Meta: RADAR, Risk Calibration, and Review Efficiency
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The proposed use of risk-ranked PRs informs reserving reviewer attention for consequential changes. The supplied annotation does not establish a safe automation threshold or the effectiveness of a deployed review route; independent defect outcomes and monitoring remain necessary.

  • W094 AI Slop is DDoSing Open Source: Understanding the Impact of AI-Generated Contributions on Open Source Sustainability
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Higher maintainer load and lower merge propensity under contribution influx inform admission limits tied to actual review capacity. Attribution and matching issues prevent claiming a universal load effect or validated queue policy.

  • W100 The End of Code Review: Coding Agents Supersede Human Inspection
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The prediction that agents can replace human-only inspection supplies a contested alternative to examine when designing a review path. No empirical test justifies removing necessary evidence, specialist review, or accountable acceptance.

  • W103 An Eye for Trust: An Exploration of Developers' Trust Perceptions Through Urgency and Reputation
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Urgency and reputation changing visual effort more than final decisions cautions against treating attention or seniority cues as evidence of better review. The manipulated labels do not establish an improved production review route.

  • W106 Code Review Agent Benchmark (c-CRAB)
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Missed human-identified actionable and architectural findings caution against replacing required review with an agent's apparent coverage. The benchmark's human-defined ground truth bounds the comparison; it does not establish every human reviewer is superior.

  • W107 Human-AI Synergy in Agentic Code Review
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Longer human-on-agent discussions and lower adoption of AI suggestions inform accounting for collaborative review burden. Discussion-selected observational PRs do not establish a causal efficiency difference or the quality of the final decisions.

  • W112 Novice Developers Produce Larger Review Overhead for Project Maintainers while Vibe Coding
    Informs practice

    The unequal review burden motivates admitting contributions against available maintainer and mentoring capacity. Lower acceptance and classified experience cannot by themselves establish an optimal review route or justify blanket exclusion of novices.

  • W147 To Ban or Not to Ban? How Open Source Projects Govern GenAI Contributions
    Informs practice

    The mismatch between inexpensive PR supply and scarce maintainer attention informs admission and review-capacity decisions. It does not establish an effective universal review policy or an optimal contribution limit.

  • W205 Who Pays the Review Cost? Triage, Fairness, and Accountability in AI-authored Pull Requests
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Reviewers' reported preference for intent, bounded scope, tests and a human owner informs defining what makes a candidate reviewable. Survey attitudes do not measure actual review time, acceptance quality or the effect of a proposed review route.

  • W208 (When) Should a Software Factory be Lights-off? Benchmarking Code Review Agents on Bug Detection
    Cautions about practice

    Bounded bug recall and poorer proprietary-code results caution against making a benchmark score the basis for unattended review. Preserve task complexity, available context and residual misses when selecting a review path.

  • W226 Large-Scale Study of GitHub Copilot Trajectories
    Cautions about practice

    Missing agent-directed intervention in public traces cannot establish that a change lacked human review. Keep review observability separate from readiness and scrutiny when using trajectory data to reason about acceptance.

Osmani (2)

  • O011 Agentic Code Review
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The shift from writing to justified acceptance informs allocating review attention to the uncertainties introduced by generated changes. It is a practitioner account of a bottleneck, not a comparative evaluation of review routes.

  • O019 Code Review in the Age of AI
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The article frames review as an accountable burden-of-proof process, informing which checks and decision owners are needed for a generated change. It supplies a review argument rather than measured evidence that more review stages improve outcomes.

Pragmatic Engineer (6)

  • P047 Learnings from two years of using AI tools for software engineering
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Birgitta Böckeler's discussion of reviewer fatigue and quality supervision identifies human review capacity as a constraint when choosing a review route. The two-year reflection and restricted remainder do not establish a measured optimal review process.

  • P085 Deepdive: How 10 tech companies choose the next generation of dev tools
    Evaluates a practice component · primary reading for this source

    The reported company-local scoring of AI review tools evaluates one component used to choose a review route: the usefulness of tool findings in that company's trial. The restricted preview and context-specific samples/scales do not evaluate full acceptance effectiveness or establish causal productivity.

    Evaluated component: Company-local scoring of AI code-review findings during tool selection; excludes end-to-end review correctness, acceptance authority and causal productivity.

  • P087 How Codex is built
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    The Codex-builder interviews illustrate tiered code review as part of an internal agent-development workflow. The retained preview does not establish the independence of its checks or comparative effectiveness of its review tiers.

  • P107 Slow down to speed up: so much has changed in 6 months’ time
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The contrast between agent-produced changes and review/reliability capacity informs limiting the review workload to decisions people can substantiate. The keynote synthesis reuses P103 and P105 material and does not provide independent confirmations of their claims.

  • P118 What is happening with code reviews?
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Routing by blast radius and retaining manual review inform selecting a proportionate review path as generated workloads grow. The preview surveys possible responses and does not establish a universally effective sequence of review stages.

  • P127 How software engineering is changing: a tale of two eras
    Cautions about practice

    The guest account's review changes, ownership changes and context-switching fatigue inform checking whether review capacity can sustain higher output. It is a single-person retrospective, not a validated recommendation to remove or standardize review stages.

    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

NDSE2 chapters (1)

  • NDSE2:C08 Code Review and Trust Calibration
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The chapter allocates human and AI review by consequence and uncertainty. It informs a review gauntlet with accountable finding disposition, coverage assessment and a separate release verdict.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Spend scarce review attention on the uncertainties that could materially change the decision to accept a candidate.

When to use it

  • Different classes of changes currently receive identical review despite very different consequences.
  • Generated candidate volume is creating a queue that exceeds meaningful checking capacity.

When to avoid it

  • A required domain approval would be replaced by a generic model review or a majority vote.

Before you start

  • A task envelope, candidate revision, and available evidence dossier.
  • Named review responsibilities and a known acceptance authority.

How to apply it

  1. Classify the candidate’s affected behavior, blast radius, reversibility, and unresolved uncertainty.
  2. Choose the smallest review path that supplies the required evidence and specialist decisions for that class.
  3. Check admission against reviewer capacity; limit new candidates when meaningful review cannot keep up.
  4. Require findings to identify a location, violated expectation, reproducible concern, or specific missing evidence.
  5. Record a verdict against the actual reviewed revision, including resolved findings and conditions that require another review.

Illustrative example

A spelling correction receives a quick scoped diff review. A change to historical payment decisions also receives contract, replay, permission, and owner review. When policy reviewers are fully occupied, the coordinator slows admission of similar candidates rather than creating a growing pile of nominally ready work. Both paths retain a clear acceptance decision appropriate to their consequences.

What to check

  • Each review stage answers a distinct consequential question for this candidate.
  • The verdict identifies the checked revision and the authority behind the decision.
  • Queue growth and reviewer workload inform admission, rather than being hidden by generation throughput.

Expected outputs

  • A risk-appropriate review route.
  • An evidence-linked verdict and any required follow-up.

Risks and failure modes

  • Unfocused comments can consume capacity while leaving the acceptance question unresolved.
  • Repeated automated reviewers may amplify a shared error instead of supplying independent scrutiny.

PAT:053PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Legacy Code Navigation

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Build a traceable map of an existing system before changing it, separating observed behavior from the intention the system is supposed to implement. Follow entry points, data, invariants, history, and ownership. Use the map to ask better questions and identify checks; a successful code search alone does not establish comprehension or authorize preservation of every legacy behavior.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Locate the knowledge needed to make a bounded brownfield change without converting implementation accidents into requirements.

When to use it

  • The codebase has unfamiliar conventions, hidden dependencies, or behavior shaped by earlier policy revisions.
  • A proposed fix depends on understanding why a seemingly redundant branch or stored field exists.

When to avoid it

  • The current evidence cannot resolve a consequential business rule; escalate the rule instead of guessing from code.

Before you start

  • Read access to relevant source, tests, history, and available system documentation.
  • A specific change question and access to the appropriate knowledge owner.

How to apply it

  1. Start from the user-visible behavior and trace its entry point, state transitions, dependencies, and outputs.
  2. Record file and revision locators for important observations, distinguishing executed evidence from reading-based inference.
  3. Compare implementation behavior with approved contracts and historical rationale; flag contradictions without silently choosing a winner.
  4. Exercise a narrow scenario or ask an owner to resolve the uncertainty most likely to affect the change.
  5. Publish a concise map, candidate impact set, and open questions that the maker and reviewer can challenge.

Illustrative example

A maintainer discovers that a replay handler returns a stored response instead of calling the current evaluator. A superficial cleanup might remove that branch. Navigation connects it to the original policy revision and the historical-response contract, then exercises an old request. The resulting map explains why the branch matters while keeping unrelated undocumented behavior provisional.

What to check

  • Important architectural claims have reproducible locators or explicit uncertainty labels.
  • The map distinguishes what the code does from what an authorized contract requires.
  • A reviewer can follow the proposed change through affected behavior and dependencies.

Expected outputs

  • A versioned behavior and dependency map.
  • A candidate impact set with unresolved questions and owners.

Risks and failure modes

  • Generated explanations can sound convincing while overlooking an indirect dependency.
  • Legacy tests and comments may encode obsolete or incorrect assumptions.

PAT:054PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Migration as Learning

Family. Architecture, Evolution and Maintenance

Use a bounded migration to examine both a system’s behavior and a maintainer’s understanding. Specify what must remain invariant, perform the representation or interface change, and independently check preservation. Evaluate what the maintainer learned through explanation and a further task; a successful migration and retained understanding are distinct outcomes that need different evidence.

3 linked sources · 1 external sources · 2 book records. Read the associations ↓

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

  • F010 Building an AI agent application to migrate a tech stack
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    The Enzyme-to-React-Testing-Library experiment illustrates examining behavior and feedback while changing a test stack, a concrete migration setting for this practice. Its failures limit reliability claims, and it does not measure a maintainer's retained learning or autonomous migration across a codebase.

  • B015 PART III: Team Workflows
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Migration as Learning in B015 (PART III: Team Workflows): OCC:NDSE:12, AI_SW_ENG/chapters_verbose/chapter07/chapter07_part3.tex lines 14–385. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:NDSE:12

  • B026 Development Practices Enhanced by AI

    The migration discussion informs the semantic-preservation component of this practice: check retained behavior with cases independent of the transformed code. The annotation does not establish learner understanding, retained skill or the effectiveness of migration as a learning exercise.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Turn a necessary structural change into an inspectable exercise in invariants and design consequences without confusing delivery with education.

When to use it

  • A migration has a manageable scope and clear behavior that must survive a new representation.
  • A maintainer needs to understand historical constraints before taking stewardship of the changed component.

When to avoid it

  • A time-critical migration would be endangered by using an unprepared learner as the sole responsible implementer.

Before you start

  • A baseline, invariant set, rollback or recovery plan, and appropriate migration owner.
  • Separate criteria for technical success and comprehension.

How to apply it

  1. Document the old and new representations, including compatibility, historical data, and transition obligations.
  2. Ask the maintainer to predict the difficult preservation cases and explain the evidence needed for each.
  3. Execute the bounded migration in a suitable environment, retaining a traceable candidate and old-state fixtures.
  4. Check the required invariants and operational transition behavior using expectations independent of the migrated implementation.
  5. Assess understanding with a new variation or repair task and record learning gaps separately from delivery defects.

Illustrative example

A team changes the storage layout of previously approved requests. Technical checks verify that old identifiers still return the originally committed responses and that conflicting payloads remain rejected. Afterwards, the maintainer explains how a second schema revision would affect replay and repairs a deliberately different mapping error. The two assessments answer separate questions about the software and its steward.

What to check

  • Preservation claims link to checks on representative old and new states.
  • The migration has a reviewable transition and recovery path.
  • The maintainer demonstrates reasoning on a case beyond the rehearsed migration.

Expected outputs

  • A migration candidate with preservation and recovery evidence.
  • A separate comprehension assessment and follow-up plan.

Risks and failure modes

  • A happy-path migration may miss historical exceptions or incompatible consumers.
  • Completion pressure can conceal learning gaps behind a successful technical result.

PAT:055PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Trio Programming

Family. Competence, Learning and Mentoring

Structure collaboration among an experienced developer, a learner, and AI assistance with explicit responsibilities. Let the learner make predictions and explain decisions, use the assistant for bounded support, and have the experienced participant protect the engineering and learning objectives. The arrangement is a mentoring method to evaluate, not a demonstrated guarantee of improved learning.

5 linked sources · 3 external sources · 2 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (5)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

5 linked sources shown

Polimi (2)

  • W120 Automation, AI, and the Intergenerational Transmission of Knowledge
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The model's expert-novice knowledge-transfer mechanism informs keeping an experienced mentor and meaningful learner participation in an assisted collaboration. It does not empirically evaluate trio programming or establish actual intergenerational labor effects.

  • W127 Remote Work Leaves Younger Workers Sidelined
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Reduced early-career access to mentorship informs checking that an experienced participant can actually guide an assisted learner. The remote-work context does not evaluate the three-person arrangement, and overlapping AI adoption complicates attribution.

Fowler website (1)

  • F005 Coding assistants do not replace pair programming
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The pairing argument informs preserving real human knowledge-sharing and collaboration when an assistant joins a mentoring arrangement. It does not assert that the discussed pairs follow the Atlas trio configuration or demonstrate a controlled learning benefit.

Earlier books (1)

  • B015 PART III: Team Workflows
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Trio Programming in B015 (PART III: Team Workflows): OCC:NDSE:13, AI_SW_ENG/chapters_verbose/chapter07/chapter07_part3.tex lines 386–660. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:NDSE:13

NDSE2 chapters (1)

  • NDSE2:C10 Developer Learning, Mentoring and Comprehension Debt
    Informs practice

    Mentoring, explanations and repairs keep the learner responsible for a mental model. They inform trio programming as a teaching design, not a demonstrated causal improvement in learner outcomes.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Combine expert oversight and useful assistance while keeping the learner actively responsible for developing and testing a mental model.

When to use it

  • A junior developer is learning a consequential code path with an available experienced mentor.
  • The team wants assisted progress while observing how the learner reasons about errors and tradeoffs.

When to avoid it

  • No participant can competently review the work, or the learner is being used as nominal approval for opaque generated output.

Before you start

  • A bounded technical task and a specific learning objective.
  • Agreed roles, time for discussion, and independent acceptance checks.

How to apply it

  1. Have the mentor frame the task, invariant, and learning goal without supplying the completed solution.
  2. Ask the learner to propose a diagnosis or plan before the assistant suggests alternatives.
  3. Use AI for targeted questions, examples, or candidate code; make the learner explain which suggestions they accept and why.
  4. Have the mentor challenge one consequential assumption and review evidence without silently taking over the whole task.
  5. Rotate suitable activities and conclude with an individual explanation or new case that reveals retained understanding.

Illustrative example

A senior engineer, a junior engineer, and an assistant inspect a replay defect. The junior predicts the failing path, the assistant helps locate relevant calls, and the senior questions whether current policy should affect stored decisions. The junior implements and explains a bounded repair. A later independent variation checks comprehension instead of treating the trio’s successful patch as a learning result.

What to check

  • The learner contributes observable diagnosis, prediction, or design reasoning.
  • Assistant suggestions are examined against code and authorized behavior.
  • Engineering acceptance and learning assessment remain separate decisions.

Expected outputs

  • A reviewed candidate with the learner’s rationale.
  • Recorded misconceptions and a suitable follow-up exercise.

Risks and failure modes

  • The learner may become a spectator while the expert and assistant exchange complete solutions.
  • Social pressure can make agreement look like comprehension.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Developer Learning, Mentoring and Comprehension Debt — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:048 · The Explainability Test
  • PAT:050 · Learning Loop Preservation
  • PAT:012 · AI-Accelerated Learning and Skill Development

PAT:056PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Parallel Work Orchestration

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Coordinate concurrent work only where tasks can be bounded, ownership is clear, and integration and review have capacity. Separate writable workspaces, define shared interfaces, and limit work in progress. Parallel production is useful only when its coordination burden is justified; adding agents does not itself divide semantic responsibility or improve accepted throughput.

8 linked sources · 5 external sources · 3 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (8)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

8 linked sources shown

Osmani (3)

  • O025 Conductors to Orchestrators: The Future of Agentic Coding
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The move from one guided agent to multiple asynchronous agents informs planning coordination and integration responsibility across concurrent work. Role forecasts and examples do not establish higher accepted throughput or future hiring outcomes.

  • O052 Your parallel Agent limit
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The limit imposed by understanding, evaluation and integration capacity informs reducing concurrency when supervision becomes shallow. Personal heuristics about agent counts and fatigue are not a validated scaling law.

  • O058 The Orchestration Tax
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    The coordination cost and scarce review time identify when additional parallel agents should be withheld or reduced. Illustrative agent counts and workload splits are not measured optima.

Pragmatic Engineer (2)

  • P070 New trend: programming by kicking off parallel AI agents
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    Practitioner accounts illustrate concurrent agent execution alongside serial review and integration attention, exposing the coordination boundary a parallel workflow must respect. The reused Sid Bidasaria conversation from P062 is dependent reporting, not another independent case.

  • P086 Steve Yegge on AI Agents and the Future of Software Engineering
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Yegge's discussion of multi-agent work and fatigue informs treating supervision capacity as a bound on concurrency. His eight-stage ladder is a provocative practitioner framework, not a validated maturity scale or Osmani's agency/orchestration axes.

Earlier books (3)

  • B015 PART III: Team Workflows
    Documents practice origin · primary reading for this source

    The retained occurrence trail locates Parallel Work Orchestration in B015 (PART III: Team Workflows): OCC:NDSE:14, AI_SW_ENG/chapters_verbose/chapter07/chapter07_part3.tex lines 661–953. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:NDSE:14

  • B025 From Single Agent to Multi-Agent Workflows
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The move to multiple agents introduces specialization, boundaries and control points. It informs orchestration decisions while requiring coordination failures and serial review to be included in throughput comparisons.

  • B095 Multi-Agent Orchestration
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The multi-agent chapter uses isolation and coordination to address an observed single-loop limit. It informs parallel orchestration while retaining integration, merge and review capacity as throughput constraints.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Allow independent work to proceed concurrently without losing responsibility for the combined behavior and final decision.

When to use it

  • A change contains genuinely separable tasks with stable interfaces or independent review questions.
  • There is enough integration and reviewer capacity to absorb concurrent candidate results.

When to avoid it

  • Tasks repeatedly modify the same behavioral target or depend on unresolved shared intention.

Before you start

  • A dependency map and named owner for each semantic target.
  • Isolated write scopes, an integration owner, and explicit admission limits.

How to apply it

  1. Separate tasks by outcome and dependency, identifying what must remain sequential or centrally decided.
  2. Assign ownership, scope, expected evidence, and an expiry or return condition for each work allocation.
  3. Provide isolated workspaces and a shared authoritative interface contract rather than copied, diverging assumptions.
  4. Admit work according to available review and integration capacity; reassign ownership explicitly when a task stalls.
  5. Integrate candidates in a controlled order, check combined behavior, and account for discarded work, reconciliation, and review.

Illustrative example

One worker improves catalogue search while another translates a separate content dataset under a frozen schema. A single owner controls schema changes and integration. If both workers discover a need to rename a field, they return that decision to the owner rather than independently changing their copies. The combined build is checked after both candidates are reconciled.

What to check

  • Each target has one current accountable owner and a visible work state.
  • Parallel tasks respect shared interface versions and do not conceal semantic overlap.
  • The integrated result passes relevant checks and the coordination effort is recorded.

Expected outputs

  • A bounded work allocation and dependency record.
  • An integrated candidate with component and combined evidence.

Risks and failure modes

  • More concurrent candidates can overload review and increase unfinished work.
  • Independent file edits can still implement conflicting business decisions.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Teams, Governance and the Engineering Organization — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:031 · Worktrees: Isolate the Write Domains
  • PAT:032 · Multi-Loop Coordination: One Owner per Target

PAT:057PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Structured Enablement Program

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Introduce AI-assisted engineering through bounded stages with observable capability, operating controls, and accountable decisions. Teach the tasks and judgment each role needs, collect evidence from an appropriate trial, and adjust the permitted scope accordingly. Course attendance or an adoption calendar can organize activity, but neither establishes that a team is ready for broader delegation.

26 linked sources · 19 external sources · 7 book records. Read the associations ↓

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Connect enablement spending with the practical ability to produce, inspect, govern, and maintain an eligible change.

When to use it

  • A team wants to adopt assistance across roles with different responsibilities and experience.
  • An existing rollout reports participation but lacks evidence of sustained engineering capability.

When to avoid it

  • Training is being used to bypass missing permission controls, review ownership, or required acceptance evidence.

Before you start

  • Named program and operational owners with a defined eligible task class.
  • A baseline workflow and observable competence and operating criteria.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the actual workflow problem and the skills needed by makers, reviewers, maintainers, and decision owners.
  2. Rehearse scoped work in a disposable environment, including failures, denied actions, and escalation rather than only successful demos.
  3. Assess individual reasoning and the team’s ability to preserve evidence, permissions, ownership, and review capacity.
  4. Run a bounded operational trial when its entry conditions hold, keeping comparable outcomes and total effort visible.
  5. Expand, revise, pause, or reduce the program against predeclared evidence; refresh it when tools, tasks, or responsibilities change.

Illustrative example

A team begins with synthetic maintenance exercises. Participants must recognize an obsolete policy fixture, preserve a failing check, and route an unresolved requirement to its owner. Only after those capabilities and the tool boundaries are demonstrated does the team try a limited set of reviewed documentation changes. Attending the final workshop does not itself authorize work on production policy.

What to check

  • Stage transitions refer to observed competence and operating evidence.
  • The program measures reviewer and maintainer capability as well as candidate production.
  • A failed condition has an owner and a route to retraining, narrower scope, or suspension.

Expected outputs

  • A staged enablement plan with entry and exit criteria.
  • A cohort evidence record and a revisable adoption decision.

Risks and failure modes

  • Calendar pressure can transform a learning stage into presumed operational readiness.
  • Training activity can look successful while review capacity or retained understanding remains inadequate.

  • Teams, Governance and the Engineering Organization — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:058PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Acceptable Use Policy

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

State what AI-assisted work is permitted, what evidence contributors must supply, who remains accountable, and how exceptions are decided. Connect the policy to enforceable controls where possible, while keeping written rules, their technical enforcement, and decision authority distinct. Version the policy and give it an owner so changing tools do not leave obsolete obligations in force.

11 linked sources · 8 external sources · 3 book records. Read the associations ↓

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make contributor and operator obligations clear enough to apply to a particular task and inspect when a boundary is crossed.

When to use it

  • AI assistance reaches shared repositories, organizational information, or externally consequential operations.
  • Teams apply inconsistent rules about tool access, evidence, disclosure, review, or responsibility.

When to avoid it

  • A generic template would be treated as a substitute for the organization’s actual decision rights and applicable requirements.

Before you start

  • An authorized policy owner and a known scope of people, systems, and data.
  • An inventory of available tools and existing review and exception processes.

How to apply it

  1. Define permitted work and prohibited effects using concrete actors, operations, data classes, and targets.
  2. Specify the evidence and contributor understanding required for each relevant risk class.
  3. Map machine-checkable rules to enforced boundaries and identify obligations that still require accountable judgment.
  4. Describe the exception path, decision owner, scope, expiry, and controls that remain mandatory.
  5. Publish a versioned policy, check its practical interpretation with representative cases, and review it after material workflow or tool changes.

Illustrative example

A project permits an assistant to prepare scoped patches but requires the contributor to understand the diff and retain relevant verification evidence. A restricted execution profile blocks writes to protected expectations and remote publication. A request for broader access goes to the named owner with its reason and scope. A sentence declaring the tool “approved” would not replace these decisions.

What to check

  • A contributor can determine which rule applies to a concrete proposed action.
  • Representative prohibited operations are denied by the relevant execution boundary.
  • Exceptions and policy changes identify a legitimate decision source and an effective revision.

Expected outputs

  • A versioned acceptable-use policy and responsibility map.
  • Enforcement mapping and a bounded exception record.

Risks and failure modes

  • Vague prohibitions can create inconsistent interpretation and invisible workarounds.
  • Disclosure or approval labels can become rituals that do not establish understanding or control.

PAT:059PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Measurement & Learning

Family. Measurement and Operational Learning

Measure the engineering workflow through a single linked event record that follows assigned work, attempts, checking, review, and accepted outcomes. Keep denominators, time windows, failures, and missing follow-up explicit. Use the observations to diagnose a bottleneck and choose the next experiment, separating descriptive monitoring from stronger claims about what caused an improvement.
