Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make apparent generation speed comparable with the total work and accepted result it actually produces.

When to use it

  • A team wants to evaluate a workflow change or explain a gap between candidate volume and delivered value.
  • Current metrics omit abandoned attempts, reviewer effort, waiting, or later repair.

When to avoid it

  • The proposed comparison changes acceptance obligations between groups and would therefore measure different outcomes.

Before you start

  • Stable task and event identifiers with clear metric definitions.
  • A defined eligible cohort, observation window, and intended decision.

How to apply it

  1. Choose the unit of analysis and define distinct events for attempts, verification, review acceptance, deployment, and follow-up.
  2. Capture active person-time, elapsed waiting, tool use, and outcome states without counting overlapping activity twice.
  3. Retain every eligible assigned item, including failures, abandonment, and work still awaiting a decision.
  4. Compare like task classes and obligations; record tool changes, familiarity, and other plausible explanations for observed differences.
  5. Report counts, denominators, missing observations, and uncertainty, then propose a focused change or measurement for the identified constraint.

Illustrative example

An assistant produces first candidates quickly, but several remain in review and two are abandoned. The ledger connects each attempt to reviewer minutes and its final disposition. The team discovers that accepted output is constrained by review capacity. It can test better review admission while keeping unresolved follow-up visible, instead of announcing a productivity gain from draft latency alone.

What to check

  • Every reported rate has an explicit numerator, denominator, cohort, and window.
  • Failures and unfinished work remain represented in the underlying ledger.
  • The conclusion distinguishes observed association, operational diagnosis, and any causal inference.

Expected outputs

  • A linked event ledger and metric dictionary.
  • A bounded diagnostic report and proposed next observation.

Risks and failure modes

  • Selective reporting of successful tasks can inflate the apparent benefit.
  • Combining person-time and queue time carelessly can double-count effort or hide the actual bottleneck.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Measuring Productivity from Code to Production — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:060PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Cost Management

Family. Economics, Infrastructure and Work

Compare execution routes using the cost of an accepted engineering outcome, including setup, clarification, review, rework, time, and infrastructure. Keep observed amounts, assumed rates, and unknown follow-up separate. A low model bill is one component of the comparison; it does not establish that an automation mechanism is economical for the whole change.

    The personal-software scenario informs considering how lower creation cost changes which small applications might be worth building. It does not measure full maintenance cost, adoption, welfare or employment effects, so those remain separate cost-accounting questions.

  • O058 The Orchestration Tax
    Informs practice

    The human work of coordinating, reviewing and integrating parallel tasks informs including those costs when comparing execution routes. The first-person account does not establish a general return on orchestration.

  • P028 Trimodal Nature of Tech Compensation in the US, UK and India
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The distinction between salary, total compensation and equity informs choosing and qualifying labor-cost assumptions when pricing engineering, review or rework. Levels.fyi submissions are not representative universal rates, and the compensation analysis does not measure an AI workflow's return.

  • P032 AI Engineering in the real world
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    The seven company accounts illustrate usage-driven LLM costs as an engineering constraint when comparing execution routes and operating burden. This preview-based link does not measure full accepted-outcome cost; the publisher's investments in two included companies remain relevant provenance.

  • P057 Creative ways to fund open source projects
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Maintenance funding and the burden of user support and contribution review inform including ongoing human work in the cost of an engineering mechanism. The reported funding options do not establish legal compliance or a universal sustainable pricing model.

    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    The Rubrik account illustrates a decision about whether shared components and their ownership justify a design-system investment. The restricted preview does not quantify full lifecycle return or establish that AI-assisted implementation removes maintenance cost.

    Cautions about practice

    The unmeasured maintenance and opportunity costs caution against treating the subscription price and coding time as the complete economics of the replacement. This personal case cannot establish a general cost advantage for generated substitutes.

    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Philip Kiely's serving techniques identify inference resources and workload assumptions that belong in the cost of an execution route. The excerpt explains batching, caching and scaling; it does not measure total engineering cost per accepted outcome.

    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The survey's reported tool costs and usage limits inform which spending constraints to include when comparing assisted workflows. The restricted follow-up shares the 906-response cohort; its interpretive developer groupings are not competency categories or causal return estimates.

  • P098 Designing Data-Intensive Applications: The Cloud & Doing the Right Thing
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The Kleppmann and Riccomini excerpts on cloud versus self-hosting inform comparing infrastructure routes with their ongoing ownership obligations. These are attributed book arguments introduced by Orosz, not a measured universal cost advantage or an AI-productivity experiment.

    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Simon Eskildsen's resource estimates inform making the infrastructure assumptions behind a design's cost explicit before committing to it. Back-of-the-envelope estimates are not observed bills or full lifecycle returns, and the disclosed podcast sponsorship remains part of the reporting context.

  • P124 Building resilient AI-powered software, and planning for when things go wrong
    Informs practice

    Visible AI costs and provider dependence inform including operating and recovery obligations when comparing infrastructure routes. The excerpt does not establish a universal return or independently audited numerical cost model.

    Informs practice

    Wide variation in AI spending informs making local cost boundaries and accepted-value assumptions explicit before setting a budget or claiming a return. Only sections 1–3 and introductory material support this link; paid company details and the final ROI discussion were not reconstructed.

  • NDSE2:C12 Economics, Jobs, Risk and Evidence-Based Adoption
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The chapter includes human effort, failed attempts, maintenance and risk in whole-loop economics. It informs cost management with a counterfactual and uncertainty bounds instead of token-price or employment-forecast shortcuts.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Decide whether an optional mechanism removes enough burden to justify its full ongoing and initial cost.

When to use it

  • A team is comparing assisted, bounded-agent, or more elaborate orchestration routes for eligible tasks.
  • Cheap attempts produce substantial review, configuration, failed work, or maintenance overhead.

When to avoid it

  • A cheaper route fails a mandatory authority, verification, or permission condition; resolve eligibility before ranking cost.

Before you start

  • Comparable outcomes, obligations, and observation windows.
  • Event-level effort and expense data, with assumptions explicitly identified.

How to apply it

  1. Define the accepted outcome and accounting boundary before choosing which costs to include.
  2. Allocate discovery, setup, execution, checking, review, integration, operations, and observed rework once to the relevant cohort.
  3. Record infrastructure allocation and active person-time separately from elapsed delay and modeled risk.
  4. Compare cost per attempt and per accepted outcome, retaining failed and abandoned attempts in the numerator.
  5. Examine which uncertain input could change the decision and collect that evidence before expanding the more elaborate route.

Illustrative example

Two workflows prepare the same class of maintenance change. One has a smaller inference bill but requires repeated reviewer clarification and more rejected attempts. The other includes a setup cost for protected checks. The team records both over the same period, separates missing follow-up from zero repair, and compares accepted-change cost before deciding whether to retain the added checker.

What to check

  • Included costs use consistent units and do not charge the same activity twice.
  • The acceptance denominator includes a defined cohort and unresolved outcomes remain visible.
  • The recommendation identifies material assumptions and a trigger for reconsideration.

Expected outputs

  • A whole-change cost model with sourced or labeled inputs.
  • A decision comparing eligible routes and their uncertain costs.

Risks and failure modes

  • Spreading fixed costs across optimistic volumes can conceal poor actual utilization.
  • Adding modeled losses to already counted rework can double-count the same event.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Economics, Jobs, Risk and Evidence-Based Adoption — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:061PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Consistency Analysis Gate

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Check whether the specification, behavioral scenarios, design, and dependent records contradict one another before admitting affected work to the next stage. Report exact conflicting claims and their consequences. Consistency is a particular gate predicate: a mutually consistent set of artifacts can still be incomplete, unauthorized, or consistently wrong about what stakeholders need.

3 linked sources · 1 external sources · 2 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (3)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Expose incompatible obligations early enough that a maker does not have to choose silently which artifact to obey.

When to use it

  • A behavior change has updated one contract view while scenarios or design records may still use an older rule.
  • Multiple artifacts describe overlapping constraints or historical behavior.

When to avoid it

  • An artifact has no defined authority or version; establish its role before treating disagreement as a substantive contradiction.

Before you start

  • Identified canonical requirements and versioned dependent artifacts.
  • A decision owner for resolving conflicts in intended behavior.

How to apply it

  1. Select the affected behaviors and gather the relevant specification passages, scenarios, and design claims.
  2. Compare their assumptions, boundaries, precedence, and version scope rather than merely matching words.
  3. Record each potential contradiction with both locators, a concrete consequence, and its decision owner.
  4. Resolve the issue through an authorized clarification or delta, then update dependent views without creating a second master.
  5. Rerun the relevant consistency predicates and retain separately any missing coverage, evidence, or authority holds.

Illustrative example

A draft says all decisions use current policy, while a scenario requires replay to preserve the originally stored response. The gate flags the two passages and an example where they diverge. The policy owner narrows the current-policy rule to new requests. A passing recheck confirms that contradiction was addressed; it does not certify every unmentioned replay edge case.

What to check

  • Each reported conflict identifies inspectable claims and the behavior they would change.
  • Resolution comes from the appropriate authority rather than an arbitrary model preference.
  • The report separates consistency status from completeness, verification, and approval status.

Expected outputs

  • A contradiction register with locators and dispositions.
  • A named consistency result for the checked revisions.

Risks and failure modes

  • Textual differences can produce false alarms despite equivalent intended behavior.
  • A shared mistaken premise can make all artifacts agree while the actual requirement remains unmet.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:062PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Research Artifact Preservation

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Preserve the source material and reasoning behind a technical decision, including rejected alternatives and unresolved questions. Create smaller navigational summaries that point back to the retained evidence. This supports future research and maintenance beyond the immediate handoff, while keeping source integrity, current applicability, and decision authority as separate questions.

4 linked sources · 3 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (4)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

4 linked sources shown

Polimi (2)

  • W186 Maintaining Mental Models: A Study of Developer Work Habits
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Difficulty recovering others' code and hidden design rationale motivates preserving explanations with their evidence and provenance. Perceived problem ratings do not quantify saved comprehension time or demonstrate the effectiveness of a preservation process.

  • W192 AIDev: Studying AI Coding Agents on GitHub
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    The reusable PR universe and curated subset illustrate research artifacts that enable later investigations. Preserve their distinct cohort identities and snapshot scope; repeated analyses of the shared data are not independent replications of an outcome.

Osmani (1)

  • O059 The Intent Debt
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Preserving goals, constraints, decision rationale and failure records informs retaining the evidence needed to reconstruct why a system choice was made. Generated explanations cannot establish historical intent, and the proposal is not a controlled drift-prevention result.

Earlier books (1)

  • B042 Advanced Patterns
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Research Artifact Preservation in B042 (Advanced Patterns): OCC:SDD1:22, AI_SDD_ENG/chapters/chapter05_patterns.tex lines 524–667. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD1:22

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Let a later engineer reconstruct why a decision was made without relying exclusively on a compressed summary or the original participant.

When to use it

  • A design choice depends on investigation, experiments, rejected options, or external source interpretation.
  • Research spans sessions and important context could disappear when the current worker finishes.

When to avoid it

  • Retention would exceed the permitted data boundary; preserve an appropriate locator and limitation instead of copying restricted content.

Before you start

  • Permitted storage and retention rules for the relevant evidence.
  • Stable source locators and a decision or investigation identifier.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the artifacts that materially support the decision, including contrary findings and unsuccessful experiments.
  2. Retain permitted source snapshots or durable locators with version, capture context, and any integrity metadata.
  3. Separate the source’s statements from the investigator’s inference and the owner’s eventual decision.
  4. Write a concise rationale linking chosen and rejected alternatives to the evidence that mattered.
  5. Record validity limits and renewal triggers, then provide the successor with an index that leads back to the preserved record.

Illustrative example

A team rejects one storage migration because it cannot preserve historical replay under an examined failure case. It keeps the candidate, scenario, result, and rationale alongside the chosen design. Months later, a maintainer can inspect whether a new requirement changes that tradeoff instead of relying on an unexplained note saying that the rejected approach “did not work.”

What to check

  • Material decision claims resolve to retained evidence or an explicit availability limitation.
  • Rejected reasoning and unresolved issues remain distinguishable from the accepted decision.
  • A successor can find the evidence needed to reconsider the choice.

Expected outputs

  • A source and experiment archive with a navigational index.
  • A decision rationale with rejected alternatives and validity limits.

Risks and failure modes

  • A summary can erase the qualification that made an original finding conditional.
  • Unbounded retention can create stale clutter or retain data beyond its permitted scope.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:063PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Parallel Implementation Exploration

Family. Architecture, Evolution and Maintenance

Build a small number of isolated implementation alternatives against the same authorized intention, then compare them using shared acceptance and next-change criteria. Keep the alternatives distinct until a responsible decision selects a route. This explores concrete designs and their consequences; it is different from asking models to debate or agree about an unchanged candidate.

5 linked sources · 4 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (5)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

5 linked sources shown

Polimi (1)

  • W202 Not All Correct Fixes Run Alike: An Empirical Study of Patch Performance in Repository-Level Issue Resolution
    Informs practice

    Different performance among functionally correct fixes motivates comparing concrete alternatives against common obligations. The benchmark does not prove that generating alternatives in parallel is economical or that the observed ranking transfers to production workloads.

Pragmatic Engineer (3)

  • P017 Cross-platform mobile development
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The platform trade-offs inform which native, cross-platform or web implementation alternatives merit a bounded comparison against shared product needs. The retained preview supplies comparison context, not an independently tested parallel-exploration method or a current framework recommendation.

  • P066 What is good software architecture?
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Matthew Hawthorne's architectural trade-offs and Netflix examples inform the criteria for comparing implementation alternatives, including operational consequences and shared responsibility. The preview does not describe a controlled parallel exploration or establish a universally best architecture.

  • P121 Why has Shopify dropped React Native?
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Shopify's reported return to native mobile development cautions against selecting an implementation approach from a framework-wide verdict. A local comparison should preserve its own requirements; one team's migration does not establish that cross-platform alternatives are obsolete.

Earlier books (1)

  • B042 Advanced Patterns
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Parallel Implementation Exploration in B042 (Advanced Patterns): OCC:SDD1:23, AI_SDD_ENG/chapters/chapter05_patterns.tex lines 668–797. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD1:23

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Resolve a consequential design uncertainty through inspectable candidates rather than relying only on competing descriptions of imagined implementations.

When to use it

  • Two materially different designs satisfy the same behavior but have uncertain maintenance or integration consequences.
  • The alternatives can be developed in isolation within a bounded exploration budget.

When to avoid it

  • The key uncertainty is missing intention, or the choice is too minor to justify multiple implementations.

Before you start

  • A shared authorized contract and independently grounded checks.
  • Isolated candidate scopes, comparison criteria, and a decision owner.

How to apply it

  1. Name the specific design question and the meaningful difference between alternatives.
  2. Freeze common obligations and compare behavior, dependency fit, migration burden, and a plausible next change.
  3. Develop the bounded alternatives in separate workspaces without giving either authority to rewrite acceptance criteria.
  4. Run the same relevant checks and examine differences in structure, assumptions, and required maintenance work.
  5. Select, reject, or request another targeted experiment; preserve the rationale and useful evidence from discarded candidates.

Illustrative example

One candidate stores policy-specific decisions directly; another introduces a generic adapter. Both must preserve historical request identity and response replay. The team exercises the same cases and asks how each would accommodate a further schema change. It may choose the simpler design, while retaining why the extra abstraction was rejected. A majority of model opinions is not the selection evidence.

What to check

  • Alternatives differ in a consequential design choice while preserving the same obligations.
  • Comparison uses the actual candidate revisions and equivalent check conditions.
  • The decision explains observed tradeoffs and records exploration and integration costs.

Expected outputs

  • Isolated candidate alternatives with comparable evidence.
  • A design decision preserving rejected-option rationale.

Risks and failure modes

  • Allowing different acceptance criteria makes the comparison unfair or meaningless.
  • Combining fragments too early can produce an unexamined third design.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Quality, Architecture and Maintainability — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:064PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Specification Scale Management

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Keep growing specifications governable through behavior-oriented slices with owners, versions, dependencies, and a single authoritative source for shared rules. Give each running candidate a precise applicable revision. Shorter documents may help navigation, but the main control is keeping distributed obligations coherent when one part changes.

4 linked sources · 2 external sources · 2 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (4)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

4 linked sources shown

Osmani (1)

  • O018 How to write a good spec for AI agents
    Informs practice

    The warning against a giant unvalidated requirements dump informs keeping specifications compact and governable as work grows. Its iterative guidance does not establish complete dependency tracking or a universal optimum for document size.

Fowler website (1)

  • F023 Understanding Spec-Driven-Development: Kiro, spec-kit, and Tessl
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Task sizing, persistent specifications and documentation overhead in the three tool explorations inform how growing specifications should be divided and maintained for brownfield work. The dated comparison does not demonstrate that more specification machinery improves delivery.

Earlier books (2)

  • B042 Advanced Patterns
    Documents practice origin · primary reading for this source

    The retained occurrence trail locates Specification Scale Management in B042 (Advanced Patterns): OCC:SDD1:24, AI_SDD_ENG/chapters/chapter05_patterns.tex lines 798–925. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD1:24

  • B068 Template Reference
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The template reference exposes the framework's document structure and artifact density. It informs managing specification scale while leaving duplication and correct intent as questions requiring separate checks.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Allow focused iterative work without copying shared constraints into inconsistent local contracts or making every change a global rewrite.

When to use it

  • A contract spans several components, teams, or independently evolving behavior slices.
  • Late changes leave active candidates uncertain about which specification revision governs their work.

When to avoid it

  • A small single-owner contract is already easy to maintain and decomposition would add unnecessary coordination.

Before you start

  • A canonical contract and explicit authority for shared obligations.
  • A way to identify slice versions, dependents, and active candidates.

How to apply it

  1. Partition by coherent behavior and assign each slice an owner, effective revision, and explicit boundary.
  2. Keep cross-cutting constraints authoritative in one place and reference them from dependent slices.
  3. Record the version bundle used by each candidate instead of allowing live documents to change its contract silently.
  4. When a delta is authorized, trace candidate impacts and distinguish changed expectations from unchanged checks that need rerunning.
  5. Hold affected stale submissions, reconcile dependent views, and review the impact set for missing relationships before resuming.

Illustrative example

A service separates new-request eligibility from historical replay while both reference a shared identity constraint. A policy delta changes new eligibility and leaves replay obligations intact. The dependency record identifies active candidates using the old ceiling. Their boundary expectations need renewal, while replay regressions still run against the changed code. No team receives an independently edited copy of the shared identity rule.

What to check

  • Every behavior slice resolves to an owner and an applicable authoritative revision.
  • Shared obligations have one source and inspectable dependent views.
  • A change identifies affected candidates and preserves the distinction between refreshed expectations and rerun regressions.

Expected outputs

  • A versioned specification map with ownership and dependencies.
  • A delta impact and reconciliation record.

Risks and failure modes

  • Excessive decomposition can hide a cross-cutting rule behind many indirections.
  • Stale or missing dependency edges can leave an apparently current candidate governed by obsolete assumptions.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:065PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Model Switching for Regeneration

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Change the model used to regenerate a candidate only after diagnosing the current failure and preserving the same authorized contract, permissions, and acceptance evidence. Treat the switch as a bounded intervention whose result must be checked. Another model may propose a different implementation, but it cannot supply missing authority or guarantee recovery from the original problem.

2 linked sources · 1 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (2)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

2 linked sources shown

Fowler website (1)

  • F029 Experiences with local models for coding
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Sensitivity to task, context and configuration cautions that changing the model is not by itself a diagnosed route to successful regeneration. Two principal tasks and uneven trials cannot establish a general ranking, and one-shot runs are not equivalent to interactive work.

Earlier books (1)

  • B042 Advanced Patterns
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Model Switching for Regeneration in B042 (Advanced Patterns): OCC:SDD1:25, AI_SDD_ENG/chapters/chapter05_patterns.tex lines 926–1107. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD1:25

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Test whether a different implementation proposal helps a diagnosed problem without silently relaxing the definition of an acceptable result.

When to use it

  • A reproducible failure persists despite a bounded repair attempt and another permitted model is a reasonable alternative.
  • The current model repeatedly chooses an unsuitable approach despite adequate task context and an external failure signal.

When to avoid it

  • The blocker is an unresolved requirement, unavailable permission, exhausted budget, or missing trustworthy oracle.

Before you start

  • The failing candidate, diagnostic, and current contract revision are preserved.
  • The alternative model is permitted for the data and has an explicit remaining budget.

How to apply it

  1. Classify the failure and identify what the switch is expected to change about the next proposal.
  2. Preserve the independent expectation, scope, protected artifacts, and spent budget across the transition.
  3. Provide the new model with the relevant evidence and failure rather than an unsupported instruction to do better.
  4. Generate a bounded replacement or repair and evaluate it with the same relevant checks and regressions.
  5. Record the outcome, incremental cost, and whether new evidence justifies further work or an escalation.

Illustrative example

A maker repeatedly repairs a threshold branch while reintroducing a replay defect. The controller supplies another permitted model with the exact failing replay case and unchanged protected expectation. Its candidate is then checked against both obligations. If it fails in the same way, the shared result points toward a deeper context or design problem rather than authorizing unlimited further switches.

What to check

  • The switch preserves the contract, oracle, permission boundary, and resource history.
  • The new attempt addresses an identified failure and produces inspectable evidence.
  • Recovery claims reflect executed results rather than the reputation or novelty of the replacement model.

Expected outputs

  • A model-switch decision and bounded attempt record.
  • Comparable verification evidence and a stop or continuation decision.

Risks and failure modes

  • A new session can accidentally discard failed attempts and reset the perceived budget.
  • Selecting the most agreeable output can replace diagnosis with unsupported model shopping.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:066PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Constitution-Driven Development

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Maintain a small set of enduring project obligations that individual feature plans must respect. Give these rules an accountable owner, revision, and change procedure; derive working views from the same authority. A constitution is stable within an authorized revision, while a reviewed delta can change it without erasing the history that explains earlier work.

3 linked sources · 0 external sources · 3 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (3)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

3 linked sources shown

Earlier books (3)

  • B042 Advanced Patterns
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Constitution-Driven Development in B042 (Advanced Patterns): OCC:SDD1:19, AI_SDD_ENG/chapters/chapter05_patterns.tex lines 110–236. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD1:19

  • B059 Constitution and Architecture: The Framework Foundation
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The framework foundation combines a constitution, architecture and controlled progression. It informs shared invariant and decision-right design while keeping design history separate from observed operational outcomes.

  • B063 Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Constitution-Driven Development in B063 (Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice): OCC:SDD2:A1, AI_SDD_ENG_V2/chapters/chapter15_patterns.tex lines 55–90. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD2:A1

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent separate tasks from quietly redefining shared constraints such as identity, historical behavior, permitted effects, and decision rights.

When to use it

  • Repeated feature work depends on a small set of cross-cutting obligations.
  • Teams duplicate important constraints into local prompts or plans that drift apart.

When to avoid it

  • The proposed constitution merely adds another competing authority to an already clear and controlled contract.

Before you start

  • An existing source of legitimate decision authority.
  • A clear distinction between shared obligations, design preferences, and task-specific plans.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the few rules that must survive individual implementation choices and explain their scope.
  2. Record each rule’s owner, effective revision, relevant exclusions, and connection to observable behavior.
  3. Make task contracts and generated views refer back to these rules rather than independently copying their authority.
  4. Treat a proposed rule change as a reviewable delta, with its reasons, affected work, and required evidence.
  5. Preserve superseded revisions and reconcile active candidates before applying the new authority to current work.

Illustrative example

A project’s shared contract requires historical request responses to remain stable. A feature plan may change the storage layout but cannot remove that obligation to simplify implementation. If the owner later authorizes a different archival rule, the change receives its own revision and impact analysis. The former rule remains available to explain the behavior of earlier accepted versions.

What to check

  • A task can identify which shared rules and revisions apply to it.
  • Rule changes have traceable authority and do not arrive through edits to derived views.
  • Historical obligations and the decisions made under them remain reconstructable.

Expected outputs

  • A concise versioned set of shared obligations.
  • A controlled delta and dependent-work reconciliation record.

Risks and failure modes

  • A sprawling constitution can turn optional preferences into expensive mandatory ceremony.
  • Treating a stable rule as eternally immutable can obstruct legitimate authorized change.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:067PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Clarify Before Plan

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Resolve consequential questions about intended behavior before committing to an implementation plan. Record each question, the work it blocks, the appropriate owner, and the effective answer. Clarification can be selective: settled work may proceed while independent questions remain open. The aim is a defensible decision, not a promise to eliminate all ambiguity.

7 linked sources · 4 external sources · 3 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (7)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Requirement-understanding failures in rejected agent PRs motivate resolving consequential intended behavior before committing to implementation. Visible GitHub coding and the shared AIDev sample do not prove every rejection has that cause or that clarification prevents it.

  • W204 Benchmarking LLM Agents for Behaviorally Adequate Test Generation from Software Requirements
    Informs practice

    Failures linked to underspecified requirements motivate resolving consequential expected behavior before relying on generated tests. The benchmark does not establish an effective clarification process or guarantee that a precise requirement yields adequate tests.

    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Avoid spending implementation effort on a plan whose central interpretation has never been authorized.

When to use it

  • A request admits materially different outcomes or conflicts with an existing constraint.
  • A design choice would implicitly settle a business rule that belongs to someone else.

When to avoid it

  • The question is a routine implementation choice already covered by the task’s authority and evidence.

Before you start

  • A scoped request and available existing obligations.
  • A way to identify who can resolve each consequential question.

How to apply it

  1. Read the request against existing behavior and constraints, separating missing facts from design preferences.
  2. Formulate the smallest concrete question that distinguishes the consequential alternatives.
  3. Record its dependency, owner, decision timing, and what can safely continue while the answer is pending.
  4. Capture the authorized answer with its effective revision and preserve any conditions or exclusions.
  5. Update affected scenarios and only then commit the relevant part of the plan; reopen clarification if later evidence changes the premise.

Illustrative example

A request lowers an approval threshold but does not mention historical replay. Before changing the replay path, the engineer asks whether existing committed responses should change. The owner confirms that only new decisions use the revised threshold and records the applicable revision. Meanwhile, an unrelated wording correction can proceed because it does not depend on that answer.

What to check

  • Each blocking question names the behavior and candidate work it affects.
  • The recorded answer comes from the relevant authority and includes applicability.
  • The plan respects the answer while unresolved independent questions remain visible.

Expected outputs

  • A question-and-decision record with dependency links.
  • An updated behavior contract and a scoped implementation plan.

Risks and failure modes

  • Asking every low-impact question can create unnecessary delay and shift routine judgment to the user.
  • A casual answer without scope or authority can be misapplied as a universal rule.

PAT:068PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Progressive Specification

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Develop and authorize a specification in manageable behavioral increments. Proceed on settled obligations, preserve explicit open questions, and version later changes through targeted deltas. Progress depends on which work is sufficiently defined and authorized, not on repeatedly rewriting a document until an automated score improves or an agent feels confident.

5 linked sources · 2 external sources · 3 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (5)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

5 linked sources shown

Polimi (1)

  • W224 Engineering Requirements for Generative AI Agents: The BARD Process Theory
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    The interview-derived cycle of scoping, building, observing and revising requirements illustrates evolving behavioral expectations through increments. It does not establish that every team uses authorized deltas or that the process is causally superior.

Osmani (1)

  • O018 How to write a good spec for AI agents
    Informs practice

    The recommendation for iterative specifications informs proceeding on settled behavior while keeping unresolved questions explicit. It does not justify repeated document rewriting as a substitute for authorized decisions.

Earlier books (3)

  • B054 The Specification Toolkits: Spec Kit and OpenSpec (openspec.dev)
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The toolkit comparison contrasts specification and brownfield change structures. It informs progressive specification and controlled deltas, without generalizing tool superiority from historical lifecycle descriptions.

  • B063 Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Progressive Specification in B063 (Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice): OCC:SDD2:A3, AI_SDD_ENG_V2/chapters/chapter15_patterns.tex lines 125–159. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD2:A3

  • B072 OpenSpec (openspec.dev)
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    The OpenSpec card represents change through packages and deltas. It informs progressively recording changed intentions while retaining the distinction between lifecycle actions and a rigid sequential process.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Support iterative delivery while keeping unsettled assumptions from silently governing implementation and acceptance.

When to use it

  • The overall problem is evolving but a useful subset of behavior has clear obligations.
  • A late requirement can be isolated into a delta with identifiable dependent work.

When to avoid it

  • The proposed slice depends on an unresolved high-consequence rule that cannot be safely deferred.

Before you start

  • A versioned intention ledger with explicit states and owners.
  • A dependency view separating settled work from blocked obligations.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the smallest useful behavior whose expected outcomes and authority are already established.
  2. Record unresolved questions with owners and dependencies instead of omitting them from the working specification.
  3. Authorize and implement the eligible slice against its pinned contract and independent checks.
  4. When new answers arrive, issue a delta that names changed obligations, affected candidates, and retained invariants.
  5. Reconcile dependent evidence and review the next slice, preserving earlier decisions and the reasons for any reopened work.

Illustrative example

A team first adds policy-version identifiers while preserving all existing responses. A later authorized increment changes the threshold for new requests. An unresolved regional exception remains explicitly outside both slices. Each candidate has its own applicable contract and checks; the team does not let a rising completeness score stand in for the missing regional decision.

What to check

  • Each admitted slice has an authorized behavior boundary and inspectable expected outcomes.
  • Open questions remain linked to the work they block.
  • Later deltas preserve history and distinguish changed obligations from unaffected invariants.

Expected outputs

  • A sequence of versioned authorized behavior slices.
  • A question, dependency, and evidence-reconciliation record.

Risks and failure modes

  • Calling a requirement future work can conceal that the current slice already depends on it.
  • Repeated regeneration can erase decisions and make progress appear to depend on document polish.

PAT:069PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Red-Team Specification

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Challenge a draft specification by constructing plausible counterexamples to its intended promises. Ask how an implementation could follow its words yet produce an unacceptable result, then record concrete gaps or contradictions for the appropriate owner. This examines the specification before or alongside coding; it is distinct from verifying that a particular implementation satisfies an established contract.

1 linked sources · 0 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (1)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

1 linked sources shown

Earlier books (1)

  • B063 Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Red-Team Specification in B063 (Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice): OCC:SDD2:A4, AI_SDD_ENG_V2/chapters/chapter15_patterns.tex lines 160–191. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD2:A4

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Expose hidden assumptions and misleading wording before they become legitimate-looking implementation choices.

When to use it

  • A specification is polished but leaves uncertainty about precedence, exceptions, state, or failure behavior.
  • A consequential rule needs examination beyond its ordinary success examples.

When to avoid it

  • The review would become an unbounded search for hypothetical issues unrelated to the authorized change.

Before you start

  • A versioned draft and an explanation of the intended outcome.
  • A bounded challenge scope and an owner who can resolve findings.

How to apply it

  1. Choose a consequential promise and identify its actors, inputs, boundaries, temporal assumptions, and exclusions.
  2. Construct a case that follows the written rule literally while violating a plausible intended obligation.
  3. Distinguish a real contradiction, an omitted decision, and a deliberately excluded behavior.
  4. Report the exact passage, counterexample, consequence, and decision needed rather than simply calling the draft weak.
  5. Have the owner resolve the issue and update affected scenarios, retaining the counterexample as a useful future check.

Illustrative example

A specification says to evaluate every request using the current policy. A challenger asks what happens when a previously committed request is replayed after that policy changes. The literal reading conflicts with historical stability. The resulting finding targets the specification’s temporal scope; it is not yet evidence that any candidate implementation contains the defect.

What to check

  • Findings contain a concrete case and an inspectable link to the challenged wording.
  • The response preserves distinctions between an approved exclusion and an unresolved obligation.
  • Resolved findings produce an authoritative clarification and a relevant observable scenario.

Expected outputs

  • A bounded set of specification counterexamples.
  • A resolution record and updated scenarios.

Risks and failure modes

  • Performative opposition can create vague objections without a useful decision or test.
  • A challenger may import an unapproved requirement and treat it as an existing obligation.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:070PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Gap-Closure Analysis

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Compare intended behavior, scenarios, interfaces, and implementation knowledge to identify candidate gaps and orphaned elements. Investigate each finding before deciding whether it represents missing coverage, an obsolete artifact, an intentional exclusion, or an unapproved assumption. Legacy observations help discover questions; they do not automatically become requirements that must be preserved.

2 linked sources · 1 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (2)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

2 linked sources shown

Polimi (1)

  • W206 When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
    Illustrates practice

    Comparing expected call-site constraints with implemented checks illustrates identifying candidate coverage gaps before repairing them. Reconstructed contracts require judgment; a missing relationship is not automatically a universally valid or complete obligation.

Earlier books (1)

  • B063 Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Gap-Closure Analysis in B063 (Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice): OCC:SDD2:A5, AI_SDD_ENG_V2/chapters/chapter15_patterns.tex lines 192–226. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD2:A5

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Turn missing traceability and uncovered obligations into specific decisions instead of indiscriminately expanding the specification to match existing code.

When to use it

  • A brownfield change has undocumented outputs, unmapped scenarios, or unclear relationships between requirements and tests.
  • A new specification may omit a consumer or preserve behavior that no longer has an authorized purpose.

When to avoid it

  • The exercise would require preserving every legacy path without checking whether its behavior is intended.

Before you start

  • A canonical behavior reference and identifiable candidate artifacts.
  • An owner for disputed meaning and a scoped impact question.

How to apply it

  1. Map the changed obligations to relevant scenarios, interfaces, implementation elements, and evidence.
  2. Flag missing relationships and apparently orphaned elements with their exact locators and uncertainty.
  3. Investigate whether each finding is an omission, a historical remnant, a valid exclusion, or a defect in the mapping.
  4. Ask the appropriate owner to resolve consequential missing behavior and record any authorized delta.
  5. Add or revise the relevant scenario, artifact, or mapping and retain unresolved items with their impact and next action.

Illustrative example

An eligibility response includes a policy-version field, but the new scenarios assert only the decision label. Analysis flags the field as potentially uncovered. Inspection shows that consumers rely on it to explain historical decisions. The owner confirms the obligation, and an independent scenario now checks both values. Other unused legacy fields are investigated separately rather than copied into the contract by default.

What to check

  • Each accepted gap has a concrete obligation or decision behind it.
  • Dismissed findings retain a reason, such as an intentional exclusion or obsolete artifact.
  • Closure adds relevant evidence or traceability without silently broadening authority.

Expected outputs

  • A classified gap and orphan register.
  • Authorized resolutions and updated coverage links.

Risks and failure modes

  • Treating all unmapped code as required behavior can preserve defects and dead features.
  • False positives can consume review capacity without improving coverage of consequential outcomes.

PAT:071PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Ambiguity Scoring

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Use an explicit rubric to organize observations about a specification’s completeness, consistency, specificity, and testability. Keep the underlying findings visible and treat critical unresolved ambiguity as a separate blocking condition. A composite score may help prioritize examination; it does not establish correctness, authorize a requirement, or supply a validated universal readiness threshold.

1 linked sources · 0 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (1)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

1 linked sources shown

Earlier books (1)

  • B063 Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Ambiguity Scoring in B063 (Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice): OCC:SDD2:A6, AI_SDD_ENG_V2/chapters/chapter15_patterns.tex lines 227–266. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD2:A6

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make a vague judgment that a specification is unclear more inspectable without replacing individual consequential findings with a number.

When to use it

  • Several draft areas need consistent review attention and their uncertainty is otherwise described only impressionistically.
  • A team wants to investigate whether a rubric could support local triage.

When to avoid it

  • A score would be used as automatic approval or as evidence that all requirements are complete.

Before you start

  • A defined rubric with observable anchors and example interpretations.
  • Separate recording of critical findings, owners, and resolution states.

How to apply it

  1. Define what each dimension means and which observable evidence supports each rating.
  2. Rate the relevant draft sections while retaining the exact gaps, contradictions, or unverifiable statements behind each score.
  3. Flag consequential unresolved questions independently of the aggregate and identify the work they block.
  4. Use the profile to prioritize clarification or review, then record whether the underlying finding was actually resolved.
  5. Before using thresholds predictively, evaluate local rating agreement and outcome relationships rather than assuming the numbers are calibrated.

Illustrative example

A draft scores well on readable structure and concrete examples, but never states whether a repeated request uses historical or current policy. The reviewer retains that question as blocking for replay work even though the overall score is high. After the owner resolves it, the record changes because an authoritative answer exists, not simply because a second model awards more points.

What to check

  • Every rating has an inspectable rationale tied to the relevant draft.
  • Critical open questions remain visible regardless of the composite score.
  • Any claim about predictive usefulness is supported by a separate evaluation.

Expected outputs

  • A diagnostic rating profile with source-linked findings.
  • A prioritized clarification list and explicit blocking conditions.

Risks and failure modes

  • Numerical precision can create confidence unsupported by the rubric’s validation.
  • Teams may optimize wording for a score while leaving the decisive uncertainty unresolved.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:072PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Handoff Chain

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Transfer the minimum state a successor needs to continue work, with links to the fuller evidence record. Each handoff identifies its inputs, output state, versions, doubts, authority, resource history, and next permitted action. The recipient checks freshness and applicability before resuming; the presence of expected files alone is not evidence that a handoff is coherent.

17 linked sources · 8 external sources · 9 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (17)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

17 linked sources shown

Polimi (6)

  • W168 Do you remember this source code?
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Reported decay of file familiarity motivates rechecking a recipient's current understanding instead of assuming earlier contribution ensures readiness. Perceived familiarity is not validated recall, so handoff reconstruction still needs concrete evidence.

  • W171 Revisiting Turnover-Induced Knowledge Loss in Software Projects
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Knowledge gaps concentrated in long-unowned files inform prioritizing what a successor must reconstruct during handoff. Code authorship is only a knowledge proxy, particularly when agents commit, so a transferred owner label is insufficient.

  • W173 Quantifying and Mitigating Turnover-Induced Knowledge Loss: Case Studies of Chrome and a Project at Avaya
    Illustrates practice · primary reading for this source

    Successor assignment in the reported cases illustrates addressing knowledge coverage when contributors leave. It does not validate the entire handoff chain, and code-blame proxies may not reflect what a successor actually knows, especially with agent-authored commits.

  • W174 Impact of Developer Turnover on Quality in Open-Source Software
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Contributor churn affecting stewardship motivates making successor responsibilities and unresolved knowledge explicit at handoff. The annotation lacks retrieved effect sizes, so it cannot quantify the benefit of a handoff protocol or the harm of turnover.

  • W185 Succession: Measuring Transfer of Code and Developer Productivity
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Lower successor effectiveness after organizational or geographic transfer motivates deliberate reconstruction of context and responsibilities during handoff. The historical corporate setting does not measure an agent-mediated handoff or validate the expanded protocol.

  • W189 The Substrate Collapse: AI Code Generation Invalidates Authorship-Based Knowledge Metrics
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Authorship-based knowledge metrics may no longer identify who can explain agent-produced code, so a handoff cannot rely on blame ownership alone. The conceptual argument motivates checking recipient understanding but supplies no empirical recalibration.

Osmani (2)

  • O013 Long-running Agents
    Informs practice

    Cross-session operation and verifiable progress inform the state a successor needs at handoff, including unfinished work and recovery information. Resumability is a requirement here, not an independently evaluated handoff result.

  • O016 14 More lessons from 14 years at Google
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Clear decision-making, communication and long-term stewardship inform what an engineering handoff should preserve for its successor. This is a thematic use of a career retrospective, not evidence that the essay describes or validates an agent handoff protocol.

    Informs practice

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Maintain continuity across people, agents, and sessions without letting compression erase constraints, failed attempts, or changed authority.

When to use it

  • Work spans sessions or passes between investigation, implementation, checking, and review roles.
  • A successor must continue from a checkpoint without replaying the entire conversation.

When to avoid it

  • The transfer would conceal that the current contract or permission state cannot be verified; stop and reconcile first.

Before you start

  • Identifiable task, candidate, contract, and evidence versions.
  • A recipient with a defined role and access to the permitted source record.

How to apply it

  1. State the current objective, completed work, candidate revision, and unresolved result in a concise structured record.
  2. Link the authoritative contract, relevant observations, failed attempts, and decision rationale rather than copying only conclusions.
  3. Carry forward consumed budget, permission scope, pending questions, and the specific next action or stopping condition.
  4. Have the recipient compare stored versions with current authority and check that referenced evidence actually applies.
  5. Acknowledge the reconstructed state, refresh stale elements, and preserve the incoming handoff as history when producing the next one.

Illustrative example

A maker stops after a replay regression fails. Its handoff includes the candidate hash, current contract revision, failing request, protected expectation, and remaining attempt budget. The next worker discovers that a policy delta arrived after the checkpoint. It preserves the old failure record but refreshes the affected assumptions before attempting a repair, instead of resuming from a vague “almost finished” summary.

What to check

  • The recipient can explain the current state and next permitted decision from the handoff.
  • Referenced evidence matches the relevant revisions and preserves open questions.
  • Budget and permission constraints survive the transfer without silent expansion or reset.

Expected outputs

  • A versioned handoff record with evidence locators.
  • A recipient freshness check and reconciled continuation state.

Risks and failure modes

  • Overcompressed summaries can erase the diagnosis that justified the next attempt.
  • Successor agents may treat historical state as current authorization merely because it persisted.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:073PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Multi-Mode Agent

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Give one agent distinct functional modes such as inspection, planning, bounded implementation, and checking, with appropriate inputs and enforced permissions for each. Record mode transitions in the controller. Changing a role prompt can change the requested task, but the surrounding system must supply the actual access boundary and preserve accountability.

1 linked sources · 0 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (1)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

1 linked sources shown

Earlier books (1)

  • B063 Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Multi-Mode Agent in B063 (Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice): OCC:SDD2:B2, AI_SDD_ENG_V2/chapters/chapter15_patterns.tex lines 299–330. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD2:B2

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Avoid exposing every capability throughout a session when different stages need different actions and evidence.

When to use it

  • A workflow alternates between read-oriented investigation and a narrowly writable implementation stage.
  • One model can perform several functions while the controller retains explicit scope and transition rules.

When to avoid it

  • A prompt-only role change would be presented as real permission isolation or independent acceptance.

Before you start

  • A controller that can enforce actual tool and artifact permissions.
  • Defined mode inputs, outputs, transition conditions, and decision owners.

How to apply it

  1. Define modes by their engineering purpose and necessary operations rather than by impressive role names.
  2. Assign the least access needed for each mode and protect authoritative contracts and acceptance expectations from the maker.
  3. Require explicit current inputs and a recorded controller decision when entering a mode or expanding permitted action.
  4. Keep the task contract, remaining budget, and evidence history stable across mode transitions.
  5. Route the resulting candidate and findings to the responsible checker or owner without letting a mode label grant acceptance.

Illustrative example

An assistant inspects a repository with read access, then proposes a plan. After the controller admits the plan, implementation mode can write only candidate files. Checking reads protected expectations and writes a separate result. These transitions are recorded and enforced. Calling the final prompt “release manager” would add no ability or authority to publish the candidate.

What to check

  • Actual denied and allowed operations match the documented mode boundaries.
  • Each transition retains the applicable contract and resource history.
  • Mode outputs identify their evidence and do not claim a decision reserved for another role.

Expected outputs

  • A mode and permission specification with transition records.
  • Scoped candidate or finding artifacts from each admitted mode.

Risks and failure modes

  • A broad underlying credential can defeat apparently narrow prompt-level roles.
  • Reusing the maker’s interpretation in a checker mode can preserve circular verification.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:034 · Safety and Guardrails: Verification Is Not Authorization

PAT:074PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Anti-Sycophancy Enforcement

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Ask reviewers to challenge a candidate with evidence-backed objections rather than agree with its author or manufacture dissent. A useful finding identifies a defect, unsupported assumption, violated expectation, or concrete investigation. Requiring critical reasoning changes the review task; it does not by itself modify model training, incentives, or the independence of the evidence.

2 linked sources · 1 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (2)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

2 linked sources shown

Osmani (1)

  • O024 Critical Thinking during the age of AI
    Informs practice · primary reading for this source

    Questions about purpose, assumptions, context and evidence inform a review task that challenges plausible AI solutions with specific objections. Critical questioning is guidance here, not evidence that a skeptical prompt removes shared blind spots.

Earlier books (1)

  • B063 Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Anti-Sycophancy Enforcement in B063 (Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice): OCC:SDD2:B3, AI_SDD_ENG_V2/chapters/chapter15_patterns.tex lines 331–362. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD2:B3

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make review informative when agreement is socially easy or fluent candidate explanations are being accepted without challenge.

When to use it

  • Review comments mostly repeat the candidate’s rationale without examining consequential assumptions.
  • A proposed decision needs a reasoned challenge before an accountable owner evaluates the evidence.

When to avoid it

  • The process demands a quota of negative comments regardless of whether a concrete problem can be found.

Before you start

  • A known candidate and an authoritative behavior reference.
  • A finding format that distinguishes observed defects, hypotheses, and preferences.

How to apply it

  1. Ask the reviewer to identify the strongest consequential assumption in the candidate or its explanation.
  2. Require a source location, counterexample, violated requirement, or proposed diagnostic for each material objection.
  3. Classify the objection by evidence status rather than accepting confident criticism as a confirmed defect.
  4. Investigate actionable concerns and retain reasons when a finding is dismissed or remains unresolved.
  5. Allow a bounded no-additional-finding result and pass the full evidence record to the named acceptance owner.

Illustrative example

A reviewer first calls a storage refactor “too complex,” which supplies little actionable information. On closer examination, it identifies that replay calls the current policy evaluator instead of returning the stored response. The latter objection names a path and a protected expectation that can be tested. If no defect is established, the review should say so rather than inventing another objection to appear adversarial.

What to check

  • Material criticism contains a traceable claim and a useful way to examine it.
  • The record separates established failures from plausible but untested concerns.
  • Acceptance depends on evidence and authority, not on the number of objections or agreements.

Expected outputs

  • An evidence-linked challenge record.
  • Resolved findings, investigations, and bounded remaining uncertainty.

Risks and failure modes

  • Performative disagreement can produce expensive false positives and discourage useful collaboration.
  • A persuasive critic can be overtrusted for the same reasons as a persuasive maker.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Code Review and Trust Calibration — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:075PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Convergence Review

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Compare a proposal, a reasoned challenge, and their supporting evidence to resolve a bounded review question. Preserve objections and the basis for any changed position instead of keeping only the final agreement. Convergence is useful when the reasons survive checking; agreement between models alone neither calibrates confidence nor proves that the candidate is correct.

2 linked sources · 1 external sources · 1 book records. Read the associations ↓

Read linked sources and relationship rationales (2)

Each link below has a reviewed meaning. External reading, author synthesis and historical origin remain distinct; none alone proves this whole practice effective.

2 linked sources shown

Polimi (1)

  • W209 Who’s Aligned to Whom? How AI Agents Shape Experts’ Research Judgment Calls
    Cautions about practice · primary reading for this source

    Experts' adoption of agent-favored analytical choices shows that agreement can reflect induced preferences rather than discriminating evidence. The causal-analysis task does not establish software-review prevalence, and defensible choices should not be relabelled as proven errors.

Earlier books (1)

  • B063 Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice
    Documents practice origin

    The retained occurrence trail locates Convergence Review in B063 (Advanced Patterns: From Frameworks to Practice): OCC:SDD2:B4, AI_SDD_ENG_V2/chapters/chapter15_patterns.tex lines 363–399. This documents the recorded historical origin, not independently verified inventorship, effectiveness, or every instruction in the expanded current guide.

    Historical locators: OCC:SDD2:B4

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make a disputed engineering decision inspectable without treating consensus as an independent acceptance oracle.

When to use it

  • Reviewers disagree about a specific tradeoff, defect hypothesis, or interpretation that available evidence could help resolve.
  • A second perspective may expose an assumption the initial reviewer did not examine.

When to avoid it

  • The missing ingredient is an authoritative requirement or an executable check, and discussion would merely defer obtaining it.

Before you start

  • A bounded question, shared candidate revision, and accessible evidence.
  • A stop condition and a named owner for unresolved decisions.

How to apply it

  1. Record the initial proposal and its evidence before exposing it to the challenger’s reasoning.
  2. Ask the challenger for a concrete counterargument and distinguish competing facts from differing preferences.
  3. Identify the observation, source, or owner decision that could discriminate between the positions.
  4. Perform or obtain that check, then record which claims changed and which objections remain.
  5. Stop when the bounded question is answered or no useful new evidence emerges; escalate unresolved consequential disagreement.

Illustrative example

One reviewer accepts a replay refactor because current tests pass. Another argues that the tests expect the wrong policy revision. They inspect the authorized historical-response contract and run an independently specified case. The first position changes because of that evidence. Had both reviewers initially agreed with the flawed tests, their consensus would not have made the replay behavior acceptable.

What to check

  • The final position is traceable to checked reasons rather than a vote count.
  • Dissenting claims and unresolved questions remain available to the decision owner.
  • The review stops according to the question and evidence, not a requirement that all models agree.

Expected outputs

  • A proposal, challenge, and evidence-resolution record.
  • A bounded conclusion or named escalation.

Risks and failure modes

  • Repeated discussion can amplify shared assumptions while appearing to increase confidence.
  • Removing dissent from the final summary can hide residual uncertainty from the reviewer.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Code Review and Trust Calibration — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality
